The bridge is an iron one, and its western end spans the track of the Pennsylvania Railroad at a point where locomotives are continually passing; and it is stated that the sulphurous acid from:the smoke stacks of the engines has been the cause of the trouble A great deal of iron above the tracks most used is being gradually eaten away, and the ground beneath is being thickly strewn with thick iron scales that have dropped from the bridge Work, which has not been protected by proper painting. Several iron posts have been weakened, and are bent in such a way as to indicate a slight move- ment of the bridge to the south. It is estimated that 812,000 or 514,000 will be required to restore the bridge to a good condition, which would probably have been saved by a first outlay for good paint. The river span, which is not reached by locomotive smoke, is not affected, and is said to be in excellent condition.—/rani. EXPLOSIVE PHYSIC.—A list has just been published, in the Union Pharnuteeutique, of accidents which have re- cently occurred during the preparation or carriage of explosive substances used in medicine. At Strassburg,a chemist's assistant was changing some lycopodium- powder from one bottle to another; the particles that escaped mixed with the air, a jet of gas was burning, and a slight explosion occurred: The frightened assist- antdropped the jar containing the lycopodium, the room was at once filled with the powder, and a violent explo- sion took place. "AS I WENT SAILING." BY THOMAS GIBBONS. / of "Boxing the Compass," "Naval Songs and Song Writers,"" The Way to Ichang," Jze. No. VIII.—THE LAND OF THE RISING SUN. Land in sight! Bearing northward, at daykht,p long grey outline of distant land had been sightedfro mast-head ; during the forenoon the cloud-like uncer- tainty expanded into the grand ,reality of "land 'close aboard," where the golden sunshine, alternating twith purple shadows, was lying in broad tracts on hilly range and delightful valley. From the deck of our vessel we traced the gradual development of objects on the shore, rejoicing the while that our storm-tossed voyage was nearly at an end. A gentle breeze, blowing favourably from the southward, carried our good ship safely up the bay of Yedo, to the anchorage of Yokohama, the chief seaport of Japan; and our first evening spent on its strand enticed ,WI into the belief, which has since; ripened into a firm conviction, that the country is one of surpassing interest and bewildering . at- tractions. The empire of Japan has a wonderful history • and during recent years, since the peaceful opening of the country, in. 1855, by Commodore Matthew C. Perry, of the United States Navy, we have frequently been brought face to face with the singular and unique people in- habiting that wonderful land. Twenty-five years ago to read of Japan was like a page of the "Arabian Nights ;" and our knowledge of it was shadowy and unreal. But there is an old and a new Japan; and certainly the course of events leads us to claim the new Japan as being of less than twenty years' growth. Within that period feudalism has died, the functions of royalty exercised byl the Shogun (general and temporal ruler) have been de- stroyed, and the rightful Emperor, erstwhile living in the retirement of his palace as the "King of Heaven," has stepped out of his seclusion to take an active part in the governing of the country. We believe that he is anxious to extend the freedom and promote the welfare of his people; and being young and impressible, supported by able Ministers, we may reasonably hope that he will yet widen that constitutionalism which he has in part in- augurated. Before glancing at other scenes and customs, we will briefly trace the traditional law by which succes- sion is secured to the throne of Japan, thereby explain- ing how the Emperor is the direct descendant of Jimmo Tenno, the founder of a dynasty more than 2,500 years old. In addition to the Empress, usually, as in the pre- sent instance, a daughter of a noble of the second degree of the first rank, it is customary to provide the Emperor with twelve subordinate wives or concubines, selected from among the daughters of noblemen about the court. No disgrace attends the position, but the custom is now regarded with disfavour; and if the present... Empress had children it would likely., enough be abolished without delay. If there should be no son 'by the Empress, the son of any of the twelve wives may be aelected to succeed to the throne. Daughters of Emperors marry one of the "four imperial relatives"—a tiainegiven to the collateral branches of the imperial house, originally the families of younger sons of Emperors. In case of total failure of heirs of the imperial body, the succession pa.ases to one of these, adopted and presented by the ' Emperor at a grand ceremonial in the presence of all the princes and nobles. The last ceremony of the kind I was observed at Tokio, August 26th, 1878, when the Prince Sawa-No-Miya, the eldest son of Azisugawa-No- Miya, was adopted as heir to the throne, previous to the Emperor's departure from the capital on a tour through the northern provinces. That ceremony of adopting a successor was one of the few lingering customs of dld Japan. Yokohama (meaning Cross Strand), on the west side of the Gulf of Yedo, about eighteen miles from Tokio, is the largest port of Japan. Until 1859 it was an insignifi- cant fishing village on a strip of land running between the waters of the bay and the Tokaido, the main road of the Empire, which stretches from the ancient Moto to the modern capital, Tokio. The settlement, built on a low level plain, extends along and back of the beach, contains many fine European buildings, and to the south- ward of it is a high bluff, upon which merchants and missionaries have erected residences and schools. "The Bluff" residences are really charming, almost all of them • have fine views of either the harbour or extensive vales, • bounded by well-cultivated slopes; or of the great Yoko- hama valley, extending away for miles, with high table land rising to ranges of mountains ha the distance, backed by the lordly Fupyama—the "peerless mountain." The snow-capped cone of Fujiyama is one of the principal sights of the land; add we have seen its bold crest, high up above the clouds, eighty miles away. The mountain is 12,365 feet high; it is not an extinct but a dormant volcano; the last eruption was in 1707. The ascent made from four points, and is tedious and straight climbing. Cultivation abounds to a height of 1,500 feet, aboie which the mountain is divided into three great belts of prairie grass and lakes, pine forests and lava. The summit is intensely Cold. The ascent is made in about six hours, while one hour only is occupied in the descent. On the mountain paths, little huts have been greeted for the shelter of pilgrims—to offer prayers to the Rising Sun from the summit of Fuji is a surety of the favour of the gods. Wealthy persons ascend the mountain quite often as religious pilgrims, and for each ascent receive a charm from the priests Of the temples. We believe the rare privilege of ascending the mountain is accorded to Japanese women every sixtieth year; but could learn nothing certain about the remarkable ex- emption.. In the fall of the year, white-clad pilgrims gatheifrom all parts of the country, staff in hand, and ' wend their way toilingly up the sacred mountain: On the west slope of the bluff, adjoining Yokohama, overlooking the valley of Homura, is the foreign ceme- tery—a plebe of historic interest. ' Many a mother's darling, men and women and children of many nations, sailors and soldiers and fortune-hunters, have there found a common resting place, and sleep sound after "life's fitful fever." A glance at some of the epitaphs reveals the stormy days and dangerous times of twenty years ago in the early period of the opening of the country. To-Clay, knowing much of the kindly nature of the Japanese, experienced in all parts of their beautiful laud, we find it difficult to understand the tales of bloodshed repeated on many a storied stone. The most imposing tomb is that of a murdered Russian officer. The bodies of Major Baldwin and Lieutenant Bird, of the 20th Regi- ment, murdered near Karnakura ; two Dutch captains, killed at Yokohama • and eleven French soldiers, shot near Osaka, are buried in the old portion of the cemetery. We copied several melancholy inscriptions, and repeat one of them here, commenting thereon, by-and-bye, as shall appear just and needful:— Sacred to the memory of C. L. Richardson, late of Shanghai, aged 28 years who was cruelly assassinated by Japanese on the Tokaido. near Kanagawa, September 14, 1882. On the day named, Mr. Richardson with two gentle- men friends and a lady, went out riding on the Tokaido, and some distance from Yokohama they found them- selves in the midst of a somewhat broken train of armed men, attending the norimonos, or palanquins, evidently occupied by persons of rank. The chief of that train was Shirnadzu Sahura' the great Satsuma noble, on his way from the capital to his province in the south of Japan. At that time it was customary for casual passengers to dismount or withdraw to a convenient distance, during the occupancy of the road by a dignitary of high station. That was the etiquette of the Japanese, and in a foreign country it is well to conform to established public customs. But Richardson disregarded the ! warnings of his friends and pushed through the head of the train; the Japanese warned him back, but he persisted in holding the centre of the road. The Satsuma retainers interpreted the act as an intentional insult to their chief, and evinced ominous signs of irritation. His companions again interposed, "Let me alone," answered Richardson; "I have lived in China fourteen years, and know how to manage these people." A soldier sprang from the ranks and motioned him back with drawn sword; he turned to obey too -late; the column closed upon him and cut him down; he was never again seen alive by his companions. They escaped; the gentlemen severely wounded, while the lady experienced the shock of great terror. We have no wish to be ungenerous to Mr. Richardson's memory, but regarding the unfortunate circumstances of his death, we fail to view it as a "cruel assassination," not- withstanding it resulted in the bombardment of Kago- shima by the English fleet in August, 1863, and the sacri- fice of hundreds of innocent lives. But military prestige had to be maintained in those days! One more epitaph, which we read on a granite monu- ment erected on the summit of the hill, near to the. cemetery gates :—" In memory of the officers and men Who went down with the U.S.S. 'Oneida,' when that ves- sel was sunk, while homeward bound, by the steamship 'Bombay,' in Yeddo Bay, Japan, January 24, 1870." The sinking of the Oneida is a story of mournful interest. "On the afternoon of January 24, 1870, the sloop-of-war Oneida left the port of Yokohama to return to the United States, after a three years' cruise. When fifteen miles , from port, in the Bay of Yedo, after the darkness' of night had set in, the Oneida was run into by the British mail-steamer Bombay, bound for Yokohama, and cut down to the water's edge." The Oneida went down by the stern in less than tenminutes,and twenty-one officers and ninety-five men went with her to the bottom." We quote an epitaph, copied from the tomb of a veteran sailor :—"ln memory of George F. Horton, deceased Aug. 2nd, 1865, aged 86 years. He was a veteran in the I American and British Navies, Peace to his Ashes. He r fought under Lord Nelson at Trafalgar and the Nile. He was with Commodore Perry in his Ist and 2nd Expe- ditions to Japan." I The scenery of Japan is universally lovely. Whore- ever we travel, through the length and breadth of the land, the most enchanting views meet the observing eye; and we remember many favoured spots around Yokohama. Our excursions extended in every direction, and our first horseback ride to the capital, in the old days before the introduction of the railway into Japan, is still a delightful memory. It was a bright sunshiny day, the heat being somewhat subdued by a refreshing breeze from the ocean. A ride on the Tokaido presents scenes With a panoramic effect. Villages hang together, one , after another, all the way to the capital; rice-fields, or pine and bamboo thickets, on either hand, fill the occa- sional openings. Every available space is cultivated ; and quaint little dwellings, sweet and clean, peep fronc-ii their hiding places among the foliage of chestnut an persimmon trees. On a warm day the habitatiOne are quite open, back and front, and the purifying breeze sweeps through the rooms; perhaps cools the earnest

CIORDON'S EXTRACT removes disagreeable symptoms But as the explorations continued, we encountered more and more ancient tombs; one of the sixth dynasty, after meals. uneasiness after food, several of the eighteenth, and even of the reign of the Heretic Kings. These latter had been violated from ancient times, and presented the appearance of a charnel- house. The inhabitants of Althmhzi, like those of Thebes, made no scruple of dipossessing,the mummies, and the extinct families, to gain possession of their tombs. Most of the chambers must have changed masters ten times before receiving their present occupants. To sum up, this was a cemetery of small people (lower classes), well- to-do citizens, priests of an inferior rank, and trades- men. The heaping-up of the bodies, and the small care with which these wore treated, would not be easily ex- plained, were it not that contemporary documents fur- nished us with the most precise information as to the manner in which the preservation and worship of the dead were regulated.- Only the rich had the privilege of occupying a separate chamber, and of ensuring, by pious foundations, the prayers of a special priest; people of fortune, and belonging to the -niddle-classes, intrusted the mummies of their defunct relatives to undertakers or contractors affiliated with the clergy, who stored the bodies in their premises, and for the payment of an an- nual rent, or a lump sum, undertook to look after their preservation, and celebrate the canonical ceremonies on the days appointed by the ecclesiastical law. . . ~ Even the animals had their hypogea, mixed with those of human beings; here are hawks in hundreds, in wooden boxes; there we find jackalls piled up in holes. The truth is, Egypt is far from being exhausted; its soil con- tains enough to occupy twenty generations of workers, and what haS come to light is as nothing.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

• Fatter TREBS.—Apples and Pears in particular require the growth of the present year reduced to three or four eyes from the bass , The strongest shoots should be taken off first, and in a fortnight or so the trees may be looked over again, when the remainder may be attended to. Advocates of the extension system of fruit culture may sneer at this summer pruning. We are as favour- able as anyone to the extension or the natural system of fruit culture, which means that the trees should be allowed to go unpruned, winter or summer, a system that answers very well in large gardeus, or where orchards are being formed. But the case is different when we come to deal with small gardens many of which are so shaded by one or two large fruit trees as to render them useless tor the cultivation of vegetables, and the mischief is aggravated where these have been planted in the centre of the garden instead of as near the outer boundary as practicable. The present is a fit- ting time to remove any extended naked and barren branches from old trees, with the view of admitting more air to those left, and inducing young shoots to come forth, as well as preserving them within reason- able bounds. ,Novices will have more confidence in per- forming the operation now than when the trees are leaf- less, and all branches appear alike to them. Apples worked on the Paradise stock, and Pears on the Quince, grow less vigorous, and do not require so much pruning, and these stocks are consequently well adapted for small gardens. Mr. Moss, of Tenterfield-street, Preston, has a small collection worked in this way in his garden at Ful- wood, which, if we recollect right, were planted last year, that are carrying a nice Ist of fruit. At the time Mr. Moss took possession of this plot there stood in it one tree that would cover his present collection of about two dozen sorts. It may be conceded that such a tree would produce more fruit than the whole of these miniatures, but it would only give a fruit season of three weeks or a month, whilst by a judicious selection of two dozen varieties the season may be extended to six months. Mdl.eover, there may be seasons when a cer- tain variety fails to fruit, whilst others, on account of their late flowering or hardier constitution, will have a good crop on, which is a weighty reason in favour of their extended culture. THE FRONT GARDEN.—The dry, hot weather has dis- posed many plants to form seeds. This is because fer- tilisation takes place with greater rapidity and certainty than in cold, moist weather. In hot weather the pollen grains and the fructifying organs are fully developed, and the former are readily wafted by the slightest breeze and brought into contact with the stigma. In fine. sunny weather the bees are busier than ever searching for honey in every expanded flower, and are active agents in conveying pollen from stamen to stigma.i ,No sooner has this occurred than the flowers collapse, and the seed vessel makes its appearance. It is then that demand is made on the energies of tho plant, but if these seed vessels are picked off as soon as formed many plants will continue to flower freely so long as other cir- cumstances are favourable. Amongst the tenants of the front garden that are particularly affected in this way are the Panay, Viola, and Sweet Peas. , The latter will cease flowering entirely as the pods approach maturity, and if we wish them to continue flowering we must pick all deeayed flowers from them. The seeds of Lupins do not interfere with the flowering of the plant during the current year, but they are so numerous and their ex- hausting action is so great that the plants must feel it the following year, and no more seed than is necessary for stock should be left on. This rule is applicable to most heavy seeding plants, and for that reason we like to Cut off all flowering stalks as soon as they become shabby. This helps to maintain a certain amount of neatness in the border as well as allowing more space between the advancing growth of other plants. THE WINDOW.—In a cottage window on the rued-side from Walton to Bamber Bridge we noticed the other day novel method of decorating the window. Two plants of the Golden Variegated Honeysuckle (Lonicera Aurea Reticulate), standing on each sale of the window inside, were trained on a breadth of trellis 4in. vide, forming an arch 15in. high. Under the centte of the arch stood a flourishing pot of Musk, and more of this redolent was planted on the surface of the soil in which the two Honeysuckles grew. The Lonicera is a native of Japan, and has survived the winter frost in numbers of Lan- cashire gardens for several years.

"John, what is the best thing to feed a parrot on?" asked an elderly lady of her bachelor brother, who hated parrots. "Arsenic ! gruffly answered John. At the opera in Dublin a gentleman sarcastically asked a man standing up in front of him if he was aware he was opaque. The other denied the allegation, and said he was O'Brien. "I suppose," said a quack, while feeling the pulse of his patient, "that you think me a humbug ?" "Sir," replied the sick man, "I perceive that you can discover a man's thoughts by his pulse." Young lady: "And how is Johnny getting on at the new school, Mrs. Scatterpole?" Mrs. Scatterpole: "Oh, beautifully, my dear! He's learning six languages— French, German, Latin, Greek. Algebra, and Euclid." "Then, if I understand you," said a merchant to a customer, "you do not intend to pay me the account you owe?" "Your understanding is correct, eap'n." "And you call yourself an honest man, do you?" "Yes, sir. If I were not honest I would tell you that I intend to pay; but being honest, I do not wish to deceive you." An honest farmer was invited to attend a party at the village squire's one evening, when there was music, both vocal and instrumental. pn the following morning he met one of the guests, who said, "Well, farmer, how did you enjoy yourself lasi. night? Were not the quartettes excellent?" "Why, 'really, sir, I can't say,' said he, "for I didn't taste them; but the pork chops were the best lever ate."

_ ' Wwor.arassa rwsrrnacYrosr oF Dons.—A number of hair. savage dogs have infested the Royal A, senal Woolwich, for ' years past. . They were apparently all of one family, and went about at night in small woks avoiding all attempts at capture. Several litters of puppies have now been des- troyed, and a pollee officer, armed with a Ole, seems to have completed the work of extermination. "ALL YE ARE BRETIIREN."—Under the head of "Our ancestors" a correspondent of Nature sends the following c nnmunication :—During eight centuries—say to the time of the Norman conquest—one's direct ancestors amount to a far greater number than would at first be contemplated. Taking three generations to a century, one has father and mother (2), grandparents (4), great grandparents (8.) At the end of the second century the number of ancestors springs to 64. Followin, the calculation you will find that at the end of eight centuries one is descended from no less than 16.000,000 ancestors Intermarriage, of course, would reduce this estimate, and there is no doubt it must have largely prevailed. But the figures are so enormous that, in spite of all, I venture to suggest that the words." All ye are brethren," are literally trite. THE LOCAL Govsarrintrei '(lttarinn) Pnoytetorra, OR- DER BILL.—The Commune' reasons for disagreeing to the amendment made by the Lords in the Local Government (Ireland) Provisional Order Bill with reference to the out- lying torrnehips of Dublin were considered, and the Mar- quis of WATERFORD moved that their lordships should not insist upon the amendment.—Lord ELPHINSTONII advised them to adhere to their previous decielon.--Lord Frrecutn- Arm was convinced øf the injustice of the Corporation of Dublin in resisting the demand of the outlying townships for an increased water supply, and suggested the appoint- Meat of a Committee to confer with the Committee of the Commons. He moved an amendment giving effect to that suggestien.—Lord Asanotutra ridiculed the idea of reviv- ing, upon a question of five gallons of water per head per day, the disused constitutional machinery of a conference between the two flonses.--.Lord WAYENEY seconded the amendment, which, on a division, was rejected by 21 to 10, and the motion accepting the decision of the Commons was agreed to. Miscsitawrous.—The County Officers and Courts (Ire- land) Plosions' Bill, the object of which was to enable the Treasury to grant pensions to County Court officers was read a•second time, and passed through its remaining stage.—The Commons' amendments to the Sea Fisheries (Scotland) Amendment Bill were considered and agreed to.—The Labburers' (Irelatd) No. 1 Bill was read a third time and passed THANES FOR THE SOUDAN TROOES?—LOId SALISBURY gave notice that next day he should move that the thanks of the House be given to General Lord Wolseley, General Graham, Lord John Hay and other officers of the army and navy, for the ability, skill, and courage with which they conducted the operations in the Soudan. The Hou.e adjourned at 5-45. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tnasnay. .

The Speaker took the chair shortly before four o'clock. THE OATHS QUESTION.—Mr. HOPWOOD gave totice that next Parliament he would ask leave to bring in a Bill to reform the law relating to oaths. QUESTIONS.—Lord GEORGE Hams:row, replying to Mr. Puleston, said a Departmental Committee had been ap- pointed to mike a report with the view of soggesting such alterations as would remedy the state of affairs in the ac- counts of the Admiralty brought to light by the recent Committee of Investigation,—Mr. W. H. SMITH informed Mr. Harris that he hoped on an early date to relieve the men in the reserve forces froua the duty of serving with the colours. Artengements would be made at once to enable married, men to return to their homes.—ln reply to Mr. Cavendish Bentinck, Sir R. Caoss said his attention had been called to the case of alleged disappearance of Eliza Armstrong, a girl under fourteen years of age,and the result of diligent inquiry had been that he thought it his duty to lay the evidence before the Attorney-General —The CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER moved that the Standing Orders be suspended with the object of winding up the business of the session.—The motion was agreed to. THE ROYAL Commostosr.—Mr. BROADHURST thee asked leave to move the adjournment of the House for the pur- pose of discussing the composition of the Royal Commis- sion on Trade Depression. Being challenged for the support of 40 members only 21 stood up. Permission was therefore refused, it being necessary that the member making the ap- plication should be backed by 40 members. Mr. Chamber- lain, Sir Charles Duke, and Sir ' Arthur Hayter, the only members of the late overnment on the front Opposition bench, did not join in the request. ROUSING OF THE WORKING CLASSES.—On the motion In go into Committee on the Housing of the Working Classes (England) Bill, hon. gentlemen who had not found an op- 'portunity of delivering-, their speeches on Monday now made them. Mr. Alderman Lawrence and Mr. Hubbard sup- ported the bill, Mr. Arnold criticising the clause relating to prison sites.. Mr. Bryce also objected to this clause, whilst generally approving the bill. Mr. Pell regretted that the measure was being hurried through at this , period of the session. Sir Sydney Waterlow supported the bill. whiph Mr. Hopwood denounced as a "crude and ill-considered measure." Mr. ALBERT GREY sarcasti- cally congratulated a Conservative Government upon pre-1 meting so socialistic a measure.—Mr;Gazzoons thought it undesirable to proceed with the bill at this late period of the sessiori, a view in which Mr. Thomasson concurred.— On the motion to go into Committee, a division waachal- longed with the result that 59 voted for further procedure, eix vntipg against it. The House then went Into Committee, a long discussion taking place on Clause 3, which proposes to make the sites of London prisons avail- able for the purposes of the bill at cost price. The various amendments to the clause being disposed of, Mr. ALBERT GREY moved to omit the clause, challenging members, with a cheerful demeanour that found no reflection in the jaded House, to "dismiss the principle from the beginning."— After some discussion the clause was agreed to, the CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER indicating an intention of meet- ing on the report stage the objections raised.—The bill ulti- mately passed through Committee. LAND PURCHASE (IRELAND) BILL —On the considera- tion of this Bill, as amended, Colonel NOLAN moved a new clause applying the Bill to grass farms.—The clause was rejected by 40 to 19.—The Bill was considered and read a third time. The House rose shortly after half•past three.

• HOUSE OF LORDS.—WEDNESDLY. The Lord Choir:moiler took his seat at two o'clock. THE WAR IN THE SOUDAN.—The House met chiefly for the purpose of passing a vote of thanks to Lerd Wolselev and other officers and the forces which under their direc- tion took part in the Nile expedition and the campaign in the Soudan.—The vote was moved by the PREMIER, who said there was no honour which the army valued so mach as the thanks of Parliament, and expressed his conviction that no expedition had better deserved the honour. This, he added, was not the moment for raising controversial topics; they most look upon the fact that the force failed in its main object through no fault of its own, but through an overrnasteriog destiny. The campaign had, in addition to the gallantry of our soldiers and sailors, displayed the great and world-wide resources of the British Empire.— Lord CARINGTON having seconded the motion, the Duke of CAMBRIDGE said he agreed with the Prime Minister in the praise he bad bestowed on all concerned, and the vote was unanimously agreed to. THE TRADE COMMISSION.—The Earl Of IDDESLE lOU 10- formed their Lordships, in reference to a statement of Mr. Broadhurst on the Trade Commission, that among the first persons he asked to serve on the Commission were Mr. Bir- twistle, who accepted the invitation, and Mr. Burnett, who declined. .
Their Lordship immediately adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. THE OPERATIONS IN THE SOIIDAN.—In proposing the vote the Cireamauoil of the EXCHEQUER said they owed it not only to her Majesty's forces but even more to them- selves not to mar the gracefulness of their action by al- lowing party differences to intrude themselves on this oc- casion. The most important and distinguishing feature of this campaign was the proof it afforded to the world of the real resources of the British Empire, and it was also memor- able as showing hew at the faintest idea of danger the colonies would rally round the mother country and fight with her soldiers under the British flag. If the Nile expe- dition did not rescue General Gordon and relieve Khartoum, it succeeded in showing that we could send from this coun- try an expedition led by able and skilful generals, backed by officers of singular ability, and composed of men of whom he could only say that they could go anywhere and do anything. The Marquis of Harenwerrox expressed his entire concurrence with the remarks of Sir Michael Hicks-Beach on the desirableness of the vote being agreed to with unanimity, and paid a high tribute to the valour displ4yed by our officers and men. Referring inci- dentally to Sir Charles Wilson's expedition. he said it was only due to that gallant officer that he should express his own opinion that the papers which had been laid before Par- liament bad justifi-d him from any imputation of delay. The campaign, said his lordship, had proved that the ancient courage of our soldiers and sailors had not in tiny degree deteriorated, and that their intelligence, their resource, and the knowledge ef their profession possessed by both officers and men had considerably increased. It had shown hew wide and various were the resources of the British Crown, and that for purposes of war as well as for purposes of peace the British Empire was not only a nams but a reality. —The motion was then put to the House, and amidst loud cheers was deeiared by the SPEAKER to have been carried

neynne contradicentc. MISCELLANEODS.—The Housing of the Working Classes Bill was read a third time.—The Educational Endowments (Ireland) Bill passed through Committee.—On the motion foeadjotirnment, Mr. BELOADHURST complained that the la. , tour. element was almost totally excluded from the Trade . . _

_ _ Commission, and contended that, t e her should be as nearly as possible an equal number of representatives of labour and of capital.—While the hon. niemberwas speaking Mr. CAL. LAN called for a (vaunt, and the Hausa was counted out at five minutes past seven. HOUSE OF LORDS.LThonsumt. The Lord Chancellor took hie seat at five -mintfies past two O'clock. Miscmatrzorrs.—On the order for the consideration of the Commons' amendments to the Housing of the Working Classes Bill, the PREMIER said that thouglahe-did not think the amendments an improvement ; it was obvious that the bill could not pass without them.—Lord BRAMwELL objected to the amendment which lAid down that there should be an implication that alionse which a tenant took was to be in a condition fit for habitation notwithstanding an express con- tract to the contrary, whereupon the PREMIER said he thought the amendment would lead to a good deal of litiga- tion, and be moved to disagree with the words "notwith- standing contract or stipulation to the contrary." This motion was agreed to, but the rest of the Commons' amend- ments were accepted. Al a later stage of the sitting it was reported that the Commons did not insist on, tba amend- ment taken exception to by their Lordships.—The Com- mons' ameedments to the Education Endowments. (Ireland) Bill were brought up and agreed to.

Their Lordships adjourned at 4-15 until two o'clock on Friday. HOUSE OF COsfMON,S.—Tnuasnev. The Speaker took theshair at three o'clock. Qtrasrions,atc.—Baron de Wooms said the report of the Loadiine Commission was now in the bawl( -of the printers. The Government did net know how the report—of which there were only two copies in existence—had got into the newspapers.—Mr. BOURKE, answering Sir G. Campbell, said the Egyptian Chamber of Notables discussed the question of the new loan and desired to associate themselves with the Government in regard to it.—The Cmarammort of the Ex- CHEQUER said there were hopes that the relief of the garri- son of Kassala Would be effected. Mr. W. al: &arra an- nounced that the Government had deeided to grant a special gratuity to the forces employed in, the Nile expedition and the active operations at Suakim, and said the cost of this grant would be covered by the Vote of Credit.—On con- sideration of the Lords' reasons for disagreeing with the Commons' amendment to the Housing of the Working Classes Bill, the Hotta SECRETARY said another bill would have to be introduced next year, and that bill would ne- cessarily include a clause providing that no house should be let in an unfit state. A Courrr Orer.—On the motion for the adjournment of the House, Mr. Callan was proceeding to call attention to the refusal to grant him a return of certain documents in relation to the Jeffries case, when Mr. KENNARD moved tbat the House be counted, and there being only 33 members present, the, House adjourned at ten minutes past four:

div.head: FOREIGN _ NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN _ NEWS.

THE FUNERAL OF GENERAL GRANT. NEW YOll%, SATURDAY.—The funeral of General Grant took place to-day, the Ceremony being of a most imposing character. The prnession left the City Hall at ten o'clock. The escort column was under the command of General Hancock, and was cotnpesed of Infantry," Marines, Bias- jackets, and Artillery; and Engineers of the United States army, together with various Militia organisations from dif- ferent States, the mijerity being from New York. The escort was followed by the hearse, which was drawn by 24 horses. All the membeis of the late General's family, with the exception of Mrs. Grant, followed in the immediate rear of the beam, and they were succeeded by President Cleve- land in a carriage drawn by six horses, Vice-President Hen- dricks in a four-horse carriage, ex-Presidents Hayes and Arthur, the members of the Cabinet, the Judges of the Supreme Court, a large number of Senatoria and members of the House of Representatives, the Diplomatic Body, the Governors of various Statee, and the Mayors of New 1 ork and other, cities. The procession was about six miles in length, and included upwards of 400 carriages, the number of persons present being estimated at nearly 100,000. To- wards the end came numerous veteran organisations and the representatives of the principal New York Exchanges. While passing the Fifth•avenue Hotel, where Mrs. Grant and the members of the late General's family are residing, the troops reversed arms, and the barrt played a funeral march. After the.completion of the religions ceremonies in Riverside Park salvos of artillery were fir,d, as well as vol- leys by the Infantry regimeets present. The whole cere- many assumed gigantic proportions, and so large an influx of visitors is probab:y unprecedented. The weather was excellent, aad but few casualties occurred during the pro- gress of the procession. Business has been entirely sus- pended throughout the day in New York, and in most other cities of the Union. The church bells tolled throughout the country, and the minute guns were fired from the war vessels lying in the HLVI,OrI river. Numerous memorial services have been held in other cities, including many in the Southern Stat,s. Among other marks of respect paid in London on Satin.- day to the memory of the late General Grant, the windows of the American Exchange at Charing Cross were draped with black. Tke Exchange was closed for the day, and the American flag was hoisted half-mast, while the blinds of the American News Room opposite the Excleknge' were drawn down, and many americans residing in the metropolis were wearing bands of crape on the left arm. The dealers In American stocks agreed not to attend the Stock, Exchange on Saturday out of reepect to the deceased. ' THREATENING MR GLADSTONE.—CONVICTION

OF BOYDELL. VIENNA, SATURDAY.--CllarleS Harry Boyden, who was arrested here a fortnight ago, was convicted to-day of.hav- log written threetening letters to Mr. Gladstone with a view to extort money. The ptisoner was sentenced to six months' hard labour. In the course of the proceedings the prisoner confessed the authors) ip of the letters to Mr. Gladstone, which had been read in court, and st dad that. his only ob- tct in writing them was to be arrested and to be sent to ondon, as he ens penniless. He further declared that at the time of writing the letters he was ill and excited. A note from the London police authorities was read, contain- ing a request from Mr. Gladstone that proceedings should not be taken against the prisoner ; and also a letter from Boydell's mother to the judge who conducted the prelimi- nary inquiry, praying for her son's release. The prisoner was defended by counsel, who addressed the court on his be- half before sentence was prononnced. MR. GLADSTONE IN NORWAY. CHRISTIANIA, 111ORSDAY.—Mr. Gladstone arrived yes- terday at Lervik, and to-day proceeds to the Nordheimsund and Odds. The right hen. gentleman is in good health. THE CHOLERA IN SYAIN AND FRANCE. MADRID, SATURDAY.—The Official bulletin reports that 4,689, cases and 1,662 deaths occurred in Spain yester• day. MADRID, MOND&Y.—The official cholera bulletin reports 4,151 cases and 1,504 deaths yesterday. MARSEILLES. SATURDAY.—Duuring the last 24 hours 88 deaths have occurred in this city, of which 30 were from cholera. MARSEILLES, MONDAY.—Daring the past '24 hours 77 deaths have occurred here, of which 35 were from cholera. The old Imperial residence has been opened since this morning as a special hospital for choler patients, under the name of the Pharo Hospital, and has received up to the pre- sent 12 sick. GIBRALTAR, MONDAY —One fatal case of illness, present- ing choleraic symptoms, has occurred in the civil hospital here. The Spanish authorities in consequence to-day sud- denly established a land cordon. A Central News telegram, dated Madrid, Thursday, says: —During yesterday 3,691 persons were attacked by cholera, and the deaths numbered 1,358. The returns, however, are again incomplete from several provinces. In Madrid yes- terday there were as many as 51 fresh cases and 25 deaths, and after the return was compiled the Cases reported showed an even greater increase, 13 fresh cases land seven deaths having been notified between midnight and three o'clock this morning. ALARMING DEATH-RATE AT MARSEILLES. A Central News telegram dated MarseilleP, Thursday. , 9 a.m., OM ,—Since Monday last there have been 200 deaths in this city, one-half of the number being due to cholera. The average of the mortality daily is greater in proportion to the persons attacked the° during the presence of cholera last year, and this fact is said by medical men to be due to the unusual heat which now prevails. A Marseilles correspondent telegraphing OR Thursday morning, said :—The eitnation is rapidly becoming worse, and unfortunately the efforts of the anthorities to conceal the true facts of the case only increase the public excite- ment. During last night there were 19 deaths from cholera. Eight of these occurred in the Pbaro hospital, while eleven others died in various houses in the town. SWISS BANK ROBBERY. ZURICH, SATURDAY.— rhe Federal Bank of this city has been robbed of a sum of 26,000 francs. THE RELIEF OF KASSALA —REPULSE OF THE

CAIRO, MOND iY.—Tb—e— S—hie-k.l) El Geden and Ras Aleola, who are in alliance, were vigorously attacked by the enemy in large numbers on the 15th July. The latter were repulsed, losing more than 300 men and their principal chief, Mobd Ibraham, besides seven others. Ras Aloola at once assembled levies for the relief of Kassafa, which is really in a starving condition.—Datly News. CAIRO, Sinzray.—Colonel Chermside telographs that he has received unofficial information from Abysinnia reporting the Abyssinnians to have been completely successful near the river Settima. ' The men of the Uhirra garrison are stated to have joined the Abyssinians, and to have arrived in Abyssinia. Ras A loola has received news from Kassala, which is reported to be satisfactory. FIGHTING AT SUAKIM.—TEIR NILE.

ALEXANDRIk, SATURDAY.—Ostuan Dignaa's troops at- tacked Suakim yesterday, hut were repulsed with ease. Our troops at Cyprus are suffering from jaundice, owing to the excessive variations in the temperature. THE GOVERNMENT'S INDIAN FINANCE.

CALCUTTA, Motrnay.-=The Madras Chamber of Com- merce has addressed a strong remonstrance to the Supreme Government on the subject of its financial policy, which it describes as presenting the appearance of being spasmodic in its movements. The reduction in expenditure and the stoppage of the cunstruction of public works to meet the cost of precautionary measures on the frontier are described as an exhibition of grave financial alarm, calculated to im- pair the credit of the country., depress the value of Govern- ment securities, and have an !undesirable effeci upon the morale of departments. THE DEFENCE OF HERAT. ' Tputtuarr, MONDAY —A letter received here from Herat, dated July 30th, states that the local authorities are buying and storing supplies of grain. in that place 2,000 men were engaged in repairing the fortifications. Great enthusiasm prevailed among the lieratis. The British Boundary Com- mission wore about nine miles to the west of Herat. The railway to Astribad will be completed in October. The authorities there are baying large quantities of grain. The Russiane,since their cenqaest of the Akhal Tekke territory, have lost 000 men there, principally owing to the heat and bad climate. SHIPPING DISASTER.-22 LIVES LOST. NRW YORK, FRlDAy.—lnt.iligence received here stated that the whaling barque Napoleon, of New Bedford, has been crushed be' ice in the Arctic regions. Twenty-two of the crew were lost.

div.head: 'LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT
div.p: 'LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT
ST. RLENS. „ ENTHUSIASTIC RECEPTION OF COLONEL

GAMBLE. The most enthusiastic politioal gathering ever held in St. Helens took place in the Volunteer Hall, Lowe- street, on Tuesday evening, when Colonel David Gamble, J.P., the Liberal candidate for the borough, made his first public appearance in his claim to the suffrages of fhe newly-enfranchised electors. Though but a few days notice of the meeting had been given, the enthusiasm among the Liberal party was most keen and earnest. This was evidenced to a remark. able extent at the gathering. Eight o'clock was the announced time for a commencement. At seven o'clock the doors of the hall were opened, and in a very few minutes the large room was densely filled. The aisles, gallery, and platform were crowded to ' thcir fullest extent, and not less than 2,000 Persons, amongst whom were a good sprinkling of the fair sex, were present. Ten minutes before the commence- .ment, Mr. Houghton, a member of the Liberal Court- ,oo, excellently sang the popular Liberal song, "Pilot of the State," the audience heartily joining in the chorus. Cheers were lustily given at the close, and in response to the encore, Mr. Houghton repeated the last verse. Punctually at eight o'clock Colonel Gamble and his immediate friends appeared on the platform, and they were received with cheers, again' and again renewed. Councillor Richard Pilkington, J.P., chairman of the 'Liberal Council, presided, and he was supported by Mr. C. Crompton, Q.C., candidate for the Leek Division of Staf- fordshire; Mr. W. R. Kennedy, Q.C., Liberal candidate for Birkknhead ; Colonel Gamble, J.e.„ nearly the whole of the St. Helens Liberal Two Hundred, and other gentlemen, in- cluding Mr. H. S. Hall, J.P.) Mr. J. C. Gamble, J.P., Mr. A. Sinclair, J.P., Dr. E. P. Twyford, J.P., Dr. Waken, J.P., Dr. Janiison, Dr. MTicoll, Dr. Ricketts, Alderman John- son, Mr. W. Gamble, the Rev. W. C. Tayler, Rev. J. John- son, Rev. J. Wilcock, Councillors John Forster, D. M.Kech- nie, A. Hanson, J. Ellison, J. Fisher, R. Belsher, and W. H.. Foster; Messrs. E. J. Simpson, M.A. (Cowley's Schools), H. It. Lacey (chairman of the Free Library Committee), 1). Gamble, jun.. Thomas Sherlock, ThomasiCrooks, George Hewitt, J. Pennington, F. W. Tinker, J. F. Booth, J. B. Leach, Thomas Roberts, B. A. Dromgoole, W. Birchall, J. Wood, John Jones, J. W. Davis, E. Abel, It Meson, J. H. Houghtoo, Thomas Glover (miners' agent), John Cross (ex. miners' agent), John M. Wilson W. Wogan, J. Houghton' (Sutten), E. W. Rawlins (Rainhill), H. A. Binney, C. C. White, J. T. Elliott, H. Martin, 1. Birchen, Slater, W. J. Cook, A. Griffin, W. J. Blinkhorn, D. Moss, Wm. Harrison, W. Hadley, E. Edwardson (Earlestown), J. Middlehurst, John Cotton (secretary to the Liberal Club), and 11. L. Riley (registration agent). The CHAIRMAN was received with loud applause. He said before they commenced the real business of the meet- kg he very much regretted to announce that Mr. Charles Russell, M.P., whose name was well known, and whom they much wished to be present that night was unable to be with them. Mr. Russell wished himself to be present, but his health was such that his medical advisers had forbidden him to come, and ordered him not to take any fresh engagements for the present. He was also sorry to announce that his brother, Lieut.-Colonel W. W. Pilkington, who went away before that meet ng was an- nounced, was not with them. He had, however, telegraphed his confidence that they would have a very successful meeting. There was also a letter of apology from Captain Duffy, who had been expected to address teem. Turning to the business of the meeting, the chairman said that he must in the first place congratulate St. Helens on that great Liberal meeting. (Cheers.) They all knew that for the first time they were face to face with an election in which , St. Helens would send a member to Parliament. (Cheers.) They all knew that in consequence of the great Reform Bill that had just been passed St. Helens was in the position in which she ought to he. (Cheers.) She was a town of 60,000 inhabitants, and, in consequenco of the passing of the bill one of the greatest bills that the English Parliament had ever passed —was able to send a representative te Westminster. He thought perhaps it was not a bad time to consider to whom they were indebted for that great right—a right that had been somehow or other withheld for many years. They all knew very well that in a short time the credit of passing that bill would be claimed by the wrong people, because they knew that the Conservative party had nothing to claim except what belonged to their Liberal opponents. He alluded to the action of Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill on the recent reform bills, and said that at the present time there was no more contemptible thing than the position of those men. Their action reminded him ef that memorable saying— A mercifui Providence fa,hioned them hollow, In order that they might their princip es swallow. (Laughter and cheers.) He thought their swallow must be greatly overloaded at the present time. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Pilkington) must go to the question—What is St. Helens going to de ? Would they return a Liberal or a Conservative? (Voices: "Colonel Gamble.") He re- minded them that that was the first public appearance of the gentleman that they hoped to see returned as a member to the House of Commons—(cheete)—and that he was able as chairman of the council of the Liberal Association to in- troduce to them his friend Colonel Gamble. tLoud cheers.) He was glad to see him there that night, glad he had been able to say "Yes" to the request of the Liberal Association that he would stand as their candidate—(cheers)--and glad to say that at the meeting of the Liberal Association he was unanimously selected as their candidate. (Cheers.) But it was for the large body of the party that night to adept him with enthusiasm, and by him carry the Liberal statidard to victory. lie did not know that it was necessary for him to say many words of recommendation as to Colonel Gamble. They all knew him. (Cheers.) Ile had lived amongst them and been connected with the trade of the town for, many, many years. To many benevolent schemes he had subscribed, and especially with regard to the public manage- ment of the town he had rendered efficient aid. He (the chairman), as a member of the Town Council, knew what Colonel Gamble had done—what earnestness and attention and time he had bestowed on questions for the interest of the town. He knew him to be an up- right and sincere man, and without any double dealing. He was in all respects a man they ought to send to Parlia- ment. (Loud cheers.) Again, he was a local man and knew the various wants connected with the trade of St. Helens. The colonel knew far mere about the trade of St. Helens—hael a far wider and stronger grasp of such a sub- ject—than almost any maa they could send; and he (the chairman) would only ask in this respect whether they could have a more worthy representative. (Cries of' No,' and cheers.) He had been a good old Liberal, and for many years president of the St. Helens Liberal Association. He had taken a leading part in the affairs of the country, and had given money from year to year for various Liberal causes. One thing be (the chairman) would tell them was that Colonel Gamble was a subscriber many years ago— possibly before many of them were born—to the Anti-Corn Law League. (Loud cheers.) To that great cause was due the cheap loaf, and it was the foundation of England's wel- fare and prosperity. He (the chairman) understood that to that great cause Colonel Gamble gave for three years no less than 10 per cent, of his entire income. (Renewed cheers.) And those things showed that he had his head screwed on the right way—(laughter and cheers)—and that his heart was in the right place. (Cueers.) Further, he was a man who would cement and join together the different shades of Liberal opinion in the tawn; and if they took him awl backed him with their enthusiasm and strength and earnestness, they would return him as their member. (Loud and continued cheering.) COl. GAMBLE, on coming forward to address the meeting,was enthusiastically received. He said : Mr. chairman, ladies, and gentlemen.-4 thank you most heartily for the hearty reception you have accorded me. I can assure you Ido not remember so good a meeting being held in St. Helens, except on the occasion when the "Grand Old Man" made his first appearance in Lancashire, when unfortunately we would not have him. I trust that the enthusiasm of this meeting may prove an earnest of the success of the cam- paign which we are just beginning, and an earnest of the energy which we shall &lOW in the work before us. (Cheers.) You all know that two months ago I was chosen as the Liberal candidate by the council of your association, and on that occasion I told the meeting all that I thought necessary,or that they chose to ask me, of my political opinions. I told them that I profesaed to have held Liberal principles all my lifrk; that I was one of the earliest Free Traders, not only because I was satisfied that the inhabi- tants of the nation which imposed Castoms duties en their imports had to paw the most of those Customs duties, but because I knew that the creating of Great Britain a free port for all the world would make it still more the workshop of the world by increasing its trade with all those countries from which it received their respective productions. I told them that I had been a consistent supporter of all the Liberal Governments during my time, and that I had supported the

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, AUGUST 15, 1885.

IA Royal Commission upon Depressed ,s'rade and Industry is, after all, to be held, pgetwithstanding that it is impossible for it to 41mand the confidence of the public, be- llse, as the Times observes, "there is only ire statesman of any note on the Commis- and that is Lord IDDESLEIGH, who has 'accepted the office of Cha;rman. It is tii4tler hard upon his lordship that, after tiVng shunted into that aristocratic siding—. House of Lords—he should be brought to do what to him cannot be other than e irksome and disagreeable task. He is a ofl'ee Trader, and, though like other leaders 11' the Tory party, he has occasionally , 1)1111oured the Fair Traders, it will not be b easant to him to find that he is being used „his party as the figure-head of what will e,anown in history as th,t Commission of te4ir Traders. BUt "needs must when a rtain old gentleman drives," and the Tory ' :als„ar,tY are just now between the old gentleman .wlei the deep sea. They dare not attempt they are in office to reverse the policy Izigich they condemned in tie most un- ti easured terms when they were in Opposi- d,°!l; and yet they want to take credit for something which will please a noisy zir'tt troublesome section of their party. They 4,not in a position to offer the Bread of a tta-ileY, and so they have fallen back upon the , e (kvice of giving the Stone of a Royal ; lit?lninission. It will come to nothing; it is I% t intended to come to anything; but 4, tic" it it may serve the Tory purpose of , ?alkling the ears of the groundlings. ' The il r Trader is the infant of economics ; he as b_ arld .cen crying for a rattle for some time; pre 't would seem to be the mission of the Wo6ent Government to provide him with one. ' ofb,afe glad to see that the leading Liberals sell: fkave been applied to have had the good tchicrie, to decline to take any part in this ' actB Play. Lord SALISBURY, With char- \ was'rk'stic inaccuracy, alleged that objection '1 nyti,'ling taken to the Cominission before il :on uing was known of its composi- tr.'s or the scope of the inquiry; but lentll4,w LEFEVRE has pulverised this state- :llkt, ,u 37 publishing the correspondence "einas taken place on the subject between t 1/4,,,at uf and Lord IppusLerort. It transpires °l4 ti.:"•r• LEFEVRE did not decline to serve 11 11°l b,e„ Commission until he found that it was , - '"' Sop to the Fair Traders, who were to it po. ',11t14,',,) o rrtei rnesentation on it altogether out of iokl it to their number or influence. He 4fo, Well say that the defence of Free Trade "At not, as was proposed, "to be left to so
10 WO e5O l''ef 111,10 I bjlrAt
II o_4,

small a minority as one or two members not supporters of the Government." In a subse- quent letter to .Lord IDDESLEIGH, he added : '• With the exception of your own name and two others, there are none in the list of nineteen which will inspire confidence in the public, or at all events in those who believe in the principles of Free Trade, while Fair Traders are represented in a very undue pro- portion." Lord HARTINGTON, when appealed to use his influence, did not hesitate to say that the composition of the Commission was "unsatisfactory, and not likely to give confi- dence to the public ;" and Lord GRANVILLE has expressed a similar opinion. Speaking on the subject in the House of*Lords on Monday night, he defended the course the Liberals had taken in declining to walk into the trap that had been set for them.

Ile asked their lordships whether they thought Mr. Goschen was a man who shirked a public duty if he thought good might come of it; and then, again, with regard to Mr. Shaw Lefevre and Mr. J. K. Cross, he believed that at first they were not un- willing to join the Commission, but when they found that it was to include seven or eight gentle- men who were Fair Traders—Protectionists he pre- ferred to call them—that there was to be a large minority of political Conservatives on the Commis- sion, and that the rest were persons representing particular manufactures, they declined to join the Commission. He was not surprised that Mr. Shaw Lefevre and Mr. Cross did not think that Commis- sion would command the respect and confidence of the country, and he did not deem it necessary to use any argument in defence of them. They were perfectly right in the course they had taken. It should be stated that, in addition to the Liberals named by Lord GRANVILLE, Mr. CounzNitY, Mr. SLAGGr and Mr. NORWOOD were appealed to, but in vain. At the last moment, Mr. BROADHURST seems to have been thought of; it would look • nice, of course, to have a representative of working- men on the Commission. But Mr. BROAD- HURST was not to be used as a cats-paw. He received an invitation so late as Tuesday last which invitation he promptly declined; and in doing so he said :—" As the interest of labour appears to have been the last consi- deration in the composition of the Commis- sion. I do not think I should now be justified in accepting the nomination." Mr. BROADHURST is quite right, and it is to be hoped that working - men throughout the country, Tory as well as Liberal, will see that, if the Government had the interests of labour really at heart they would have written to such men as Mr. BROADHURST somewhat earlier. Mr. BIRT- WISTLE, secretary of the Weavers' Associa- tion, seems to have been honoured with an invitation before one was sent to the member for Stoke ; but as Mr. BIRTWISTLE is a Tory it is not perhaps unnatural that he should have been thought of in the first instance. Lord DUNRAVEN will be happy on the Com- mission, surrounded as he will be by such out- and-out Fair Traders as Mr. FARRER ECROYD Mr. W. H. HOULDSWORTH, Mr. P. A. Muwrz, and Mr. N. LUBBOCK. But what can be the value of the opinion of such a body of men? They have already given ex- pression to their "lame and impotent con- clusions ;" and it can add nothing to their worth when they are placed in a Blue Book. They are for the most part mad on the ques- tion of Fair Trade ; but there is method in the madness of some of them. Mr. EcRoYD, for instance, has been sorely punished as a manufacturer by French competition. He would be delighted if the Government could be induced to take steps whereby French, goods could be kept out of English markets. WILLIAM FARRER ECROYD would not trouble himself about the consumers of Great Britain and Ireland having to pay more for articles of clothing if he could act on lago's advice and put money in his purse. Like most Fair Trade notions, it would ' be a very "fir thing" for him, but very unfair for everybody else. And so with Mr. MUNTZ ; he is in the sugar trade, and advocates a countervailing duty.; that is to say, he wants to grow rich by increasing the prize of sugar. He would I soon be in for a " sweet thing "if he could have his way; but it would mean "sour pie " for the rest of the community. Fortu- nately these Fair Traders are seen through; we are not yet a nation of lunatics ; and we can afford to look on and smile at the game which is about to be played by the chief members of the latest Royal Commission.
i"

THE Liberals of St. Helens had a magnifi- cent meeting on Tuesday evening in support of the candidature of Colonel DAVID GAM- BLE, who has been unanimously selected to fight the battle of Liberalism at the next election. Unlike his opponent, he is a townsman, with a splendid record of past services. He is known and trusted; and is in every way worthy of the distinguished honour which, we believe, St. Helens will confer upon him in electing him as its first representative. To us it presents itself as bordering on the impertinent for a Tory to come before the electors of such a constitu- ency. For years St. Helens has been quoted, not by Tories, but by Liberals, as the largest town in the Kingdom that had no representa- tive in Parliament. If the Tories had had their way, those who are about to be called upon to give a vote, for the first time would still have been out in the cold; and under these circumstances, if working-men are loyal to themselves, or have any sense of grati- tude, they will give their votes to those who gave them the franchise. So far as local claims are concerned, Mr. SETON-KARR is not in the running with Colonel GAMBLE. Where was the Tory candidate when Colonel GAMBLE, in order that the starving poor might have cheap bread, was, year after year, contributing one-tenth of his income in sup- port of the Anti-Corn Law League? Where was he when, as President of the Liberal Association, Colonel GAMBLE, in purse and person, was fighting the battle which has resulted in Two Millions of people—the men of St. Helens included being brought within the pale of the British Constitution ? Where was he when the Liberal candidate put his name down for £ oo to swell the Irish Famine Fund, and added to that by giving so per cent upon all subscriptions above, £l,OOO ? We cry, " Where ?" and, as Mr. SETON-KARR has no voice in these matters, Echo answers, " Where " BO it may be said Liberals do not, as a rule, put forth claims of this kind in support of a caudidate. Granted ; it is more in the way cf Conservatism ; but we want the electors to see that, taking the Tories on their own ground, they havn't a leg to stand on. If we turn to the programme of the future, it will be seen that Mr. SETON- KARR has really nothing to offer. He can indulge, as Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL did on Wednesday, in vague promises about good government; but let anyone try to lay hold of something tangible, and he will find that he is grasping at a shadow. Colonel GAMBLE, on the other hand, has clear views of the re- forms he desires to see carried out, and they are reforms which, we do not hesitate to say. will commend themselves to the common

sense of all classes of electors. He is So far in Favour of civil and religious liberty that he would alter the law so as to leave it optional for a member of Par- liament to take the oath or to affirm. Valuable as the Employers' Liability Act has been found, he recognises that it can be im- proved ; and he is in favour, too, of an amendment of the Mines Regulation Act. Whilst thoughtful of those at home, he is I not forgetful of those at a distance, and is therefore anxious to assist in passing a Crofters' Holdings Bill which shall deal justly with the struggling peasantry in the Highlands. He looks to a reform of Local Government for remedying many abuses in England as well as Ireland, and he would put the break on the House of Lords in such a way as to render the peers harmless for the future. It is hardly necessary to add that he would abolish the law of primogeniture, and make other important changes with a view to setting the land free ; while as to taxation he holds to the principle he has always advo- cated—that of equalising the burden so that the rich shall have their share as well as the poor. With such a candidate, and with such a programme, we cannot believe that St. Helens will do other than honour itself by returning a true and tried Reformer to the reformed House of Commons.

WE are glad to see from cases heard at the police courts that penalties for adulteration are occasionally enforced. But it would be well if raids on law breakers of this class were more frequent; for when there is laxity in carrying out the law offenders find that it pays them to run a certain amount of risk. A milk dealer named RYLA.NCE was brought before the St. Helens magistrates the other day and fined ten shillings and costs for sell- ing milk that was watered to the extent of i 5 per cent. Mrs RYLANCE pleaded that she herself bought the milk, and had retailed it just as she had got it. But this, of course, was no defence; she has her remedy if she does not get what she orders. The public must be protected; and left, if they like, to water their own milk as they water their whisky. In another case, heard at the same Court, there was evidence of a landlord water- ing his whisky over-much. GEORGE WIL- COCK, of the Nag's Head Inn, was summoned and fined for supplying whisky which was five degrees weaker than allowed by the Act of Parliatnent. The solicitor who defended urged that his client had put in the proper per-centage of water and no more; it had re- mained in the keg for a fortnight, and "the constable purchased the last quart in the keg." The inference was that the spirit had got the upper hand of the water, which had sunk to the bottom. Poor, weak water; it is always getting put on. What a pity it is that milk dealers and publicans can't leave it alone! Saperintendent JOHNSON remarked that it was in consequence of complaints that he had he sent a constable to the Nag's Head, whereupon the solicitor observed that "if somebody had a little bit of spite they knew what to do." This, as it seems to us, is " a hard saying," for it implies that pub- licans are all sinners in watering their whisky; all that is needed is that the police should be put on their track. This is surely going too far ; but, spite or no spite, publicans, like other citizens, have only to observe the law and they may then defy the police. At the Newton Police Court, on Saturday, there was a charge of adulteration of another kind —that of selling butterine for butter. The defendant, Mr. JOHN HOWE, contended that the article sold as butter had been purchased by him as pure butter, and a question being raised as to the analysis, the case was ad- journed. TENNYSON in !' Maud" says that "chalk and alum and plaster are sold to the poor for bread, and the spirit of murder lurks in the very means of life." But Since he wrote his celebrated poem scores of articles besides bread have become debased by adul- teration. And so we have a law to put down adulteration, and, having such a law, it must be enforced.

ITHE BEGGING NUISANCE AT RUNCORN.—OII Wednesday, at the Police Court, Stephen Bowen and Catherine Bowen, man and wife, were convicted of begging in Bridge-street on the 11th hist and were each sentenced to 14 days' hard la- bour. RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.—A sitting of this court WAS held on Tuesday before His Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, when there were 2 adjourned cases, 16 original plaints, and 13 judgment summonses. There were no cases of public interest. THE BEGGING NUISANCE AT RUNCORN.—Far some weeks pest Runcorn has been literally infested with beggars, but I the police are rapidly " clearing them out." On Monday William Henry Fenton, Michael O'Hara, John Mayo, Mar- garet Jacksoe, and James Stewart were charged with beg- ging in various parts of the town. Evidence was given by Constables Finney, Bryan, Wallace. and P.S. Neild, and each prisoner was sentenced to seven days' hard labour. Tun WIDNES Poirefesma. Mr. W. Dannett. poet- master of Widnes, has been appointed to take charge of the St. Helens post office in place of the late Mr. Grey. Mr. Dannett has held his present position for five years, and was for 28 years in the Warrington post office, being chief clerk for a third of that period. His unvarying courtesy and kindness and attention to duty will cause his departure to be greatly regretted by the public. TEE HARVEST.—Corn cutting was commenced on Wed- nesday in the Widnes district, when a fine field of oats be- longing to Mr. Peter Longton was submitted te the sickle. The harvest this year premises to be a very abundant one notwithstanding the prejudicial character of the atmosphere. permeated as it is so frequently with the noxious vapours from the various chemical works. Nangolds, turnips, and other roots are in a very healthy state, and potatoes are abundant and free from disease. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, when there were peesent Messrs. W. Littler (chairman), James Handley, li'., G. Moss, T. Nor- man, E. Imison, W. Muller, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary). The Financial Committee reported that the receipts for tee past month amounted to £43 16s 9d. The interments for the four months ending July 25th were 127, against 107 in the corresponding period of 1884. The fees received for the melte period amounted to £l3l 55, showing an increase of £l2 2s 9d. . SEVERE STRUGGLE WITH A PRISONER AT WIDNES.—OR Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Michael Clarke, a labourer, was charged with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C. Townley. At a quarter to one on Tuesday morning the constable took the prisoner into custody in Mersey-street for being drunk and disorderly. On the way to the station he behaved very violently and kicked the officer on the legs many times. A struggle of an hour's du- ration took place. At the station he had to be held down whilst he was searched.—He was fined in the total of 15s and costs, or, in default, 21 days' hard labeur. ALLEGED THEFT OF ZINC AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, Catherine Hynes, Martin Can- non, and Stephen Power, all under 15 years, were charged with stealing a quantity of zinc from Messrs. Hutchinson's Chemical Works.—Lawrence Canninghein, labourer, of Ditton, saw the prisoner Hynes in the yard at the works on Saturday, and when she left he missed a block of zinc. P.C. Holbrook found two blocks in the yard of one of the pri- soners, and two near the gate of the works. Hynes, in re- ply to the charge, said "It is not only me but Martin Can- non and others." Power said "We may as well tell the troth. We have stolen them all week and got lid each off ' Mrs. Kerley."—The prisoners were remanded for a week. A RUNCORN BEERSELLERS' REVENGE.—Much amuse- ment has been caused in Runcorn during the past few days ,by the novel method adopted by a local publican to bring , ' his defaulting customers ".to book." Outside his door he had posted a long list ef names of well-known persons and the amount they owed for their worship to the "flowing I bowl" was stated. It was boldly headed with the announce- went that "the following are a mean and shabby lot." Many defaulters used rather expressive language on finding that boniface had "got 'ern on the list." and it is stated 1 that several old scores have been settled. Mine host threatens that if terms are not made with him several other persons will be exposed. PRESENTATION TO THE REV. B. HARPER, OF WIDNES... An ordinary meeting of the Mission band in connection with Victoria-road Wesleyan Chapel was held on Thursday evening, when Mr. S. Wilkinson, on behalf of the Mission, , presented the Rev. R.. Harper, the superintendent minister, with a handsome silver-mounted walking stick and a travelling bag as an earnest of the affection with which he was regarded by the young men of the society. Mr. Har- per, who was unacquainted with the intentions of the Mis- sion, suitably replied. Addresses were delivered by Messrs. Q. Pickthall, W. Taylor, W. Rigby, J. Haddock, D. Davies, , S. Read, A. Cooper, George Davies, &c., touching upon Mr. Harper's character and services to the Wines Weslevans. Mr. Harper will preach his farewell sermon to-morrow (Sun- ' day) evening before departing to his new circuit. CRUELTY TO 1 HOUSE AT WlDNES.—William Hooker was brought before the Widnes magistrates on Wednesday charged with cruelly illtreatinv a horse by working it whilst in an unfit state. Evidence was given by Sergeant ' Strickland to the effect that on the 31st July the defend- ant's horse was drawing a cart heavily laden with butcher's meat along Waterloo-road. On tne right shoulder of the animal was a woued. from which matter was oozing, larger than a 5s piece, and the small collar the horse had on WAS pressing against the sore and c ausing the horse much pain. It was an old wound, and the defendant said the horse had had an accident a week before.—lnspector Wood and P.C. 1254 gave evidence as to tbe wound and the pain the animal suffered.—The defendant said the sore was healed up when he put the horse in the shafts, and he denied that the cart was laden.—He was fined 103 and costs. 14s, or seven dm. . A DRUNKEN MAN'S CHALLESOR AT WIDNES.—David Hatton, an elderly MAIL living in Deck-street, appeared be- fore the Widnee magistrates on Wednesday charged with being drunk and disorderly in Dock-street.--P.C. Lamb de- posed to the defendant'a condact In the street, and P.C. Evans said half an hour previously the defendant's wife fetched him to the house, stating that her husband had another woman in the house, and bad turned her out. The defendant made use of most violent language towards him. —The defendant, in a very noisy fashion, contended that he never left his house, as be knew they would "fetch him there" if he did. He put his foot upon the doorstep, and told Constable Evans to put his foot to his and put up his hands, sad he would see what he could do. The police- man said, Come outside, and I will show you what I will do with you." He called his wife, who, to his astonish- ment, said he was drunk, but added that he never went ) further in the street than the doorstep.—The Bench imposed a fine of 5s and costs, 7s 6d, or seven days. GOOD TEMPLARY AT WIDNES.—The weekly session of ehe Widnes Samaritan Lodge 1.0.G.T. was held on Mon- day evening, the W.C.T., Brother Machin, presiding. Five new members were initiated into the lodge, and the usual I routine business was transacted. Subsequently an enjoy- able entertainment took place. Bros. Wright and Ilewson and Sister Annie Lamb contributed songs in capital fashion, and the W.C.T. gave a reading entitled "The Slaves."— The Excelsior Lodge Degree Temple held a special session on Thursday night for the purpose of conferring degrees and electing officers for the ensuing six months. Brother Jones presided. Degrees were conferred upoe two candidates in third degree, and upon six in the second degree. The following officers were appointed ;—D.T., Bro. Galilee; D.V.T., Sister Prescott; P.D.T., Bro. Bowden ; D.S., Sister Turton ; D.F.T.. Bro. Machin ; D.T., Bro. Pearson ; D.C., Sister Greig ; D M., Bro. Kirkham; D.G., Bro. Jones; D.Sen., Bro. Widders ; D.D M., Sister Smith; D.A S., Bro. Evans. The ceremony of installation was performed by Bro. T.S. Machin, T.D.G.W.C.T., of Runcorn. in an impres- sive manner. Ibe following officers have been appointed to the Hope of Appleton Lodge :—W.C.T., Bro. T. Ray ; W.V.T., Sister A. Thompson ; W.S., Bro. T. Harrison; W.F.8., Bro. J. Whitefield ; W.T., Bro. W. Hill; W.C., Sister E. Hill ; W.M.. Bro. R. Leather ; W.G., Bro. , Roberts ; W. 5.11., Bro. J. Hornby. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A MARINE STORE DEALER.— Before Messrs. John Brock, H. S. Hall, and H. Gaskell, 1 jun., at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Alice Kerley, , marine store dealer, Nelson-street, and her son Peter, aged about 14, were brought up in custody charged with having between the Ist and the 10th inst. received a quantity of zinc, well knowing it to have been stolen from Messrs. Hut- chinson and Co's. chemical works.—Andrew McConky, fore- man at Messrs. Hutchinsones works, and who lives at 96, Mersey-road, said there were a large quantity of zinc blocks similar to those produced at the works. During the past few weeks a great many had been stolen. They were worth lOs 6d per cwt.—ln answer to Mr. Knowles, who appeared , for the prisoners, witness said he could not swear that the ' zinc produced belonged to his firm—P.C. Holbrook deposed to apprehending the prisoners at Runcorn on Tuesday. She sail"l know what you have come for, but I went out of the way so that I could give my books into the lawyer's hands. I have bought zinc, lead, and inclia-rubber many a time, but I cannot write ; my son does all the writing." Afterwards he searched the premises of the prisoner and found a block of zinc concealed amongst some cinders beneath the stairs. When charged with the offence, the woman replied "I have never seen that piece if I was going to die." The boy said" There was no zinc in our house. Was that got on our premises ?" —Mr. Knowles contended that there was no case against the bey.—On the application of Inspector Wood, the prisoners were remanded for a week, and bail was refused..

PHOTOGRAPHING A PRISONER.—On Friday morn- ing, the young man giving his name as John Rakin, Gerard-street, off Byrom-street, Liverpool, charged with stealing £4B from Martha Oates, of the Fleet- wood Arms, Runcorn,was taken to a photographer's in Warrington for the purpose of having his " pic- ture " taken. He "pulled his face" into all sorts of shapes, and it took several men to hold him when the photograph was being taken. The police evidently look upon him as an old offender. JOSEPH MAZZINI, a memoir by E. A. V., with two essays by Mazzini : (1) "Thoughts on Democracy;" (2) The duties of man."
