THE BITE OF • DOG: CL•IX FOR DAIDGEB.—An action arising out of injuries sustained by the bite of a dog was heard at the St. Helens County Court. before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, jndge, on Wednesday. Patri. k Cosgrove, a chemical labourer. at Simm's Cross sought to recover the sum of £l2 from Thom.s Gerard, landlord of the Alexandra Vaal N., Victoria-read, Widnes, for damages in respect of in- juries received by his wife, whe was bitten on the band by defendant's dog.—Mr. H. la. Riley, who appeared for the complainant, said that on the 21st May Mrs. Cosgrove was passing defendant's house, when his dog suddenly jumped from the-step, and without the slightest provocation seized her hand and bit the third finger very severely.. Her finger bled profusely, and she went to Dr. Booth, who cauterised the wound. Mrs Cosgrove, immediately after she was bitten, went into Gerard's house, and hear! his wife saying that the dog would have to be parted with, as it bad bitten one of their own children and another man. Defendant had since destroyed the dog, and paid the doctor's bill. Mse Cosgrove suffered a great deal, and was not able to attend to her household duties for five weeks. During that time she had to engage her sister and pay 2a a day with her meals, making 4s a day for 30 days, which she felt she was entitled to.—Mrs. Cosgrove then gave evidence in suppost of Mr. Riley's statement, which was supported by Charles Wilson, nephew of Mrs. Cosgrove, and Mrs. Elizabeth Broaden, sister of Mrs. Cosgrove.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, who ap- peared for the defendant, sail his client denied that it was a savage or ferocious dog. It WAS a valuable greyhound, which had made a name in cssursing circles, and it wee worth £lO or £5O. After the dog had bitten Mrs. Cosgrove, the latter's hesband made a bargain with defendant that if the dog was destroyed and Vie doctor's bill paid, no further claire should be made against the defendant. The defen- dant had accordingly destroyed the dog, and paid the doc- tor's account.—The defendant, Thomas Gerard, supported . Mr. Swift's statement, and denied that his wife had ever made the eratements alleged by Mrs. Cosgrove in respect to the dog having bitten his daughter or any other person.— P.C. Liptrot said he was present when the parties made the agreement stated by Mr. Swift.—Hik Honour thought that the plaintiff's husband arranged with the defendant on his own behalf and on behalf of his wife for the destruction of dog and the payment of the doctor's bill, and then there should be ne further claim against the defendant. He did not think the arrangement was a wise sane for either party.— Judgment was entered for the defehdant. without costs.

NEW LANCASHIRE JUSTICES.—On Friday morn- ing the names of the following gentlemen were in- serted in the i of the peace :—Mr James Wild, Oldham; Mr. Abraham Crompton, Cromp- ton; Mr. Joseph C. Lees, Oldham; Mr. Robert Meller, Royton ; and Mr. Edward Wright Wrigle, Oldham, for the county of Lancaster; and of Mr. William Alexander Abram, editor of the Blackburn Times, for the borough of Blackburn. A CURIOUS PORTRAIT TRANSACTION.—At the Liverpool County Court Messrs. Blake and Macken- zie, lithographic printers, sued Messrs. Leng and Co., proprietors of the Sheffield Daily Telegraph, to re- cover £5O. The plaintiffs recently got up a sheet containing portraits of "leading provincial jour- nalists," and reduced fac-similes of the journals owned or edited by them, each gentleman pictured paying .£5O for the honour, and having 1,000 copies of the sheet to distribute. Mr. Leng, the editor of the Sheffield Telegraph, complained that his portrait was not a faithful one, and his firm refused tb pay the plaintiffs, hence the action. The judge entered judgment for the defendants, with costs. We may add that Dr. Mackie, of Warrington, was amongst those who subscribed for a portrait in this series. THE HOME IRON TRADE.—There has been no great change in the English iron market since we last reported upon its condition. In the pig-iron trade there is a sluggish demand, with prices far from steady. In the Glasgow warrant market quo- tations have been maintained, but the turn-over has not been large, and there is no change to note in the position of affairs. Scotch makers have recen- tly been selling More freely, but the largest sales have been of iron for 'storing purposes. Closing sellers were pn Wednesday 41s 3id cash and 41s 5d one month; buyers offering id per ton less. The pig-iron trade of the North of England has been very flat this week, and little business has been done. The inquiry has been almost nil, as there are few buyers. Makers' prices are usually about 32s No. 3 prompt, and merchants are 31s 10id, the lat- ter asking 32 for forward delivery.—lron. A WARRINGTON SOLICITOR AND HIS DITTIES. —A curious dilemma has arisen at Hale in connection with the holding of an inquest upon the body of Mr. Frank Leece, of Birkenhead, who was drowned in a yacht race at Eastham on the 20th June. It seems that Colonel J. Ireland Blackburne, by reason of some manorial rights which were confered upon his ancestors during the reign of King John, him- self possesses the powers of coroner for the manor, but not wishing to perform the duties appertaining to the office, he has appointed Mr. Buckton, solici- tor, of Warrington, to act in his stead. This gentle- man, unfortunately, has been away on a visit to the Continent, and could not possibly arrive back before Thursday night. Consequently, as he has no deputy, the inquest could not take place until Friday morn- ing. Inquests in Hale are so few and far between that the idea of providing for any contingencies may not have presented itself to the mind of Mr. Buckton ; but, all the same, his absence has caused no little inconvenience. Having been in the water for over six weeks the body is in a very advanced stage of decomposition. On Friday Mr. 'Buckton held an inquest on the body of Mr. TL,eece, salesman to Messrs. Littledale and Co., of Liverpool. The body was identified by an intimate friend of the de- ceased from Douglas. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. COMPLIMENTARY DINNER TO AN AMERICAN NEWS- PAPER PROPRIE'rOR.—Mr. Ernest King, news- paper proprietor, of Middletown, Connecticut, U.S.A., formerly of Blackburn, and proprietor and editor of the Blackburn Times whose visit to England we re- ported several weeks since, has returned from his natiie county of Bucks, where he has been staying with relatives, and is now about to return to his home in America. On Monday, a few old friends of Mr. King whilst he resided in Blackburn, desiring to have a day together in his company before his departure, invited that gentleman to join them in an excursion into Ribblesdale. Ingleton was the first place chosen for the jaunt. which being reached by Lancashire and Yorkshire and Midland Railways soon after noon, dinner was served to the party, numbering about a dozen, at the Ingle- borough Hotel. Mr. B. Abbott was in the chair. and Mr. Nutt all, of Hollins, Darwen (Mr. King's brother- in-law) in the vice-chair. After dinner the Chair- man gave the health of the guest, Mr. Ernest King, in a short but very complimentary speech. The health was drunk with much heartiness, and Mr. King responded, reciprocating friendly manifesta- tions, and spoke briefly of American politics, and of the exigencies of journalism in American cities. Mr. Hewitson (Preston Chronicle), Mr. Abram (Blackburn Times), Mr. Walker (Warrington Examiner), and Mr. L. S. Walmsley followed with brief expressions of their gratification in meeting Mr. King once more, and with good wishes for his future welfare. The afternoon was spent in strolling about the quaint old Yorkshire village, and, in visiting the waterfalls at the head of one of the romantic wooded ravines which open out at Ingleton. The party returned to Blackburn by the 6-30 train from Ingleton. Fine weather, lovely scenery, and good company com- bined to render the excursion exceedingly agreeable. —Blackburn Times.

T.;;;- TA; OF LOCAL CLlCEGY.—Writing to the Liverpool Daily lost, a correspondent signing him- self " A Church Mouse," says :—" I observe that Dr. Ryle holds some remarkable opinions as to the liv- ings of the incumbents in his diocese, about 200 in all. He said that these gentlemen might be said to occupy, far more than enjoy, their livings, their amounts were so small; or words to that effect. Bishops have certainly peculiar opinions as to the clergy. Dr. Benson told us recently that one of their most beautiful characteristics was modesty. Dr. Ryle tells us now that poverty, or something not far off, is the badge of that tribe of Levi, at least in his diocese. As a commentary on the statement, let us reckon up several of the livings in Lancashire, most of them in his diocese, and the rest in that of Manchester. Justice, like charity, shall begin at home, and with Liverpool, incumbent Mr. Stewart, his (the Bishop's) chaplain, £2,000; Walton, two incumbents, dividing £2,111; Sefton, E. Honey, £1,824; Wigan, Canon Bridgeman, £1,400; Stan- dish, W. R. Brandreth, for 44 years owner and in- cumbent, £2,000; Halsall, B. H. Blundell, £3,500; Bury, E. J. G. Hornby, 35 years rector, £1,937; Prescot, H. A. Macnaughton, £1,200; Winwick, F. G. Hopwood, for 30 years, £3,500; Croston, 0. Master, £1,038; St. Helens, Mr. E. Carr, £665; Sutton, Mr. Valiancy, 36 years, £716; Huyton, Mr. Penrhyn, £705; Rufford, Mr. Goggin, £600; .C 23,196. These 15 clergy- men receive, even on the" average "so often quoted by bishops, about £1,600 each every year in one English county, with many others below four figures." Other instances followed, and the corres- pondent concluded :—" As regards brethren in Lan- cashire, two at least receive as much as Dr. Ryle himself, and earn it for more easily, as a section of 1729 persons in the parish of Win-wick, and 1,700 in Halsall, will show. This last living is in Lord ; Derby's gift; but how Standish, with its great , revenue, became a piece of property (rimed , by the incumbent himself would be interesting to know. Such instances exist in the church by the hundred, but the amounts are much smaller. kiaßßlSTEßS—wbose professional labours neCesSitafe long In- terval, between meals—nothing will be found so exhilarating, comforting, and capable of sustaining exhausted natwe as Cadbury's Cocoa, guaranteed absolutely pure.—Advt.

SERMON AT WIDNES.-00 Sunda', morning, at St. Mary's. and in the evening at St. Paul's, the Rev. W. W. Pomeroy, M.A., Association Secretary of the London Society fer pro- moting Christianity among the Jews, preached to good con- gregations in aid of the society. WESLEYAN TREAT AT WIDNES.—The annual treat to the children of the Wesleyan schools was a failure owing to the heavy rain that fell on the occasion, and the committee gave them a second treat on Saturday. About 500 sat down to tea in Lacey-street school, and afterwards headed by the Soap Works Band and with flags flying they walked in pro- , cession to a field at Appleton, lent by Mrs. Deacon. The I weather being fine, a pleasant time was spent. SUDDEN DEATH IN A CRICKET FIELD AT WIDNES.— Henry Shaw Hearne, 18 years of age, a joiner, who lived at 19, Witt-road, Widnes, died on Saturday afternoon whilst playing cricket in a field near Ross-street. lie was walking from one wicket te the other, when be fell, and died in a few minutes. Dr. MacLennan was sent for, but his services were not required. The young man had been recently treated for heart disease. The Coroner considers an inquest unnecessary. Femmes ete A RuNconx MERCHANT.—A. meeting of the creditors of Mr. James Hallows, who traded under the style of the Runcorn Smelting Company, was held on Wednesday at the offices ef the Official Receiver, Liverpool. The debtor's liabilities were stated to be £14,819, and the assets were estimated at £3,727. The Insolvency was attributed to loss in works and shrinkage in the value of metals at Runcorn. Mr. Hallow% was adjudicated a bankrupt, and Mr. Lewis Voisey, of 30, North John-street, and Warring- ton, was appointed a trustee. A committee of inspection was also nominated. SPORTS LT RUNCORN.—The sports in connection with the Runcorn Football Club were continued on Saturday after- noon, when a 220 yards handicap was run for gold and silver medals. First heat: 1, T. Johnson, 4 yards; 2, J. Clarke, 18 yards. Second beat: 1, G. Wainwright, scratch; 2, T. Acton, 6 yards. Third heat: 1, P. Riley, 14 yards 2, J. Jones, 16 yards. Fourth heat: 1, H. Speakman, 16 yards; 2, E. Lunt, scratch. Final heat: 1, H. Speakman; 2, E. Lunt; 3, J. Clarke. The final in tho football contest, six aside, resulted in the victory of W. Hughes' team over the team of W. Dunbavand. SAD END OF A. WOMAN AT RUNCORN.—On Monday, Mr. T. J. Ridgway, coroner, held an inquest at the Board Office, Runcorn, upon the body of Martha Acton, who was drowned at the docks on Friday nightl Mr. Samuel Yar- wood was foreman of the jury. From the evidence it ap- peared that a week previous the deceased, who was an im- moral woman, 25 years of age, was released from Knutsford Gaol, and came to Runcorn, where she took up her resi- dence in a house of ill fame in Penketh-lane with Ellen Jackson, Polly Wilson, dm. On Thursday she met George Foggard, mate of the flat "Gertrude," who lives at Riga. street, off Irwell-street, Manchester, and arranged to meet him on the following afternoon. She did so, and in the evening got very drunk, and agreed to live with Froggard on his boat. Accompanied by Ellen Jackson they started from Polly Wilson's at a quarter past midnight. Jackson left the couple at Devonshire Square, and they went on to , the tidal deck. In order to get to the "Gertrude," it was I necessary to cross two schooner, the first of which was about four feet from the quay side. Foggard went on the I vessel to get a plank to bridge the space, and in his absence the woman attempted to jump on board, and fell between the quay and the vessel. She immediately sank, and did not rise again to the surface. The body was recovered with grappling irons about two o'clock by P.C. Fryer. Evidence was given to this effect by Ellen Jackson, David Price, sea- man on board the "Guiding Star," George Foggard, and P.C. Fryer. A verdict of found drowned was returned. CATTLE DISEASE int CuEsnrnE.—The weekly statement of the Chief Constable of Cheshire as to cattle disease in that county for the week ending the Bth instant shows that 24 animals have been attacked during the week with swine fever. The disease has appeared on 13 fresh farms in the town- ships of Ashton-upon-Mersey, Bollington, Bollin Fee, Chorley, Cogshall, Dunham Massey, Lymm and Odd Rode. The animals affected were immediately slaughtered. An AMERICAN CONGRESSIkfAN. - Hon. Martin A. AUDACIOUS ROBBERY FROM A LADY.—At the Borough Court, on Monday, a young man who gave the name of John Ranking, and who was described as clerk to a Liverpool betting man, was charged with stealing from the person of Mrs Martha Oates, in the Market-place, on the previous afternoon, a purse containing the sum a £4B lOs in gold.— Chief-constable Hunt said that Mrs Oates was the wife of Mr. Oates, of the Fleetwood Arms Inn, Run- corn, and the defendant said that he lived in lodg- ings off Scotland-road, Liverpool. About half-past three o'clock on the previous afternoon Mrs Oates accompanied by a lady friend, was in the market opposite Mrs Massey's greengrocers' stall. The two were looking at some fruit. Mrs Oates had with her a satchel, hanging on her left arm, and the purse was placed in that receptacle. Mrs Oates felt a kind of jerk when she was looking at the fruit, and then observed that her satchel was open and the purse gone. A young woman near pointed to prisoner and said "That young man has taken it: Mrs Oates and her friend followed and laid hold of pri- soner, who was then noticed to adroitly drop into the open satchel the sealskin purse produced. He said to Mrs Oates "Do not have me taken up' I have got a wife and family." Mr. Place, faarket 'inspector, then approached and prisoner was given into custody. The purse contained £4B lOs in gold. Prisoner wished him to believe that he was a man of previous good character, and he (Mr. Hunt) wished for a remand, to give time for inquiries to be made in respect to prisoner.—The Bench granted the remand, and Major Litton, who presided, re- commended prosecutrix to be more &refill in future than to go in a public market with so much money in her satchel.

A WRECKED FISHING BOAT.

At the St. Helens County Court, on Saturday, before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, judge, and a special jury, an action was heard in which Henry Dunbabin, fisherman, of Snake, sued Samuel Kennerley, of Otterspool, another fisherman, for damages for alleged trespass, the detention of a fishing boat, and the loss of property it contained.—Mr. J. 0. Swift ap- peared for plaintiff, and Mr. Dodd, barrister, represented defendant —Mr. Swift sta.ed that in February last plaintiff had a boat which be called the "Royer of Spate." It was registered on the 3rd June, 1884, and on the 14th February it was moored in the river close to his own house, fastened with a chain and padlock. Next day, from what he was told, he went to the river and found that the boat was miss" log. He gave information to the police, and he and a con- stable made search, the result being that the boat Rover of Spoke was found on the shore close to defendant's house. Oa examining the boat they discovered that a number of things, including including 30 cwt. of iron ballast, had been taken away. The cabin door had been broken open and the pad- lock was gone, Kennerley produced the lock, after which he was taken into custody on a charge of stealing the boat. The Prescot magistrates committed him to the assizee, where he was acquitted. After the discovery of the boat in defen- dant's possession plaintiff teek it home, but defendant, with a number of others, came again and took it 'AT, saving it was his. Mr. Swift added, in explanation of how plaintiff became possessed of the boat, that in 1883 a man named Thomas Ball, of Garston, saw something in the river, which turned out to be the keel of a boat, with stem and stern post attached. He got them on to the shore, and afterwards sold them for 5s to plaintiff's son. Thirty pounds' worth of material was purchased, and the boat in dispute was con- structed. Mr. Dodd contended that the boat never really belonged to plaintiff. Defendant had a boat called the Hannan, which was lost in the river in 1878, and the Rover of Speke was the very boat repaired. Be called Malcolm Bell, boat builder, of Liverpool, who said that six or seven Years ago he entered into a centract with defendant to alter the Hannah. The boat in dispute was the same boat. It was woith about £5O when be saw it, but it was not then in such working order.—By the Judge : There could not have been £3O worth of new material put into it since he altered it —Defendant said he identified the boat as the ll ab bY its general appearance. It must have been drawn out of the river.—His Honour said the first question for the jury was whether any portion of the old boat was deferidant'e at all. They would remember that the boat was lost in 1878, and not found again until 1883 For five years it had apparently been embedded in mud or tossing about the Mersey. Defendant and his witness lerofessed to identify it by certain marks. If they had satisfied the jury that any part of t was defendants, then they would effect to it in their consideration of the case, but if they s.atisfled that any part of it was defendant's, then twg clearlyevaretet not i verdict must go for plaintiff. If no part of the boat belogged to defendant, he had no right to touch it at all, and he would be responsible for any damage done by his away, and the second time of his doing so would i aggravate the damages which they would give to o in respect of the defendant. The jury had to decide between the conflicting witnesses as to what really we re the of the case. If they were satisfied that any pt iendl o a tv if t ei t it belonged to defendant, then it was only a que;- to lion of damages. If it was merely timber, the remains of an old boat, plaintiff would only be liable to the defendant for the value of the timber when he used it for his new boat. But in that case plaintiff would be equally entitled to re- cover damages against the defendant for the removal of the boat, because the boat was made by plaintiff. But if the jury believed the material that was found in 18$3 was a boat, although a damaged one, and that all the plaintiff did was to repair it, then plaintiff must put up with the loss of his trne, labour, and materials, and could not recover against defendant for his resuming possession of his own property. The acquittal of the defendant at the as,izes did not help them to form any seund opinion as to the rights of the parties. That o. ly showed them that judge o- jury were satisfied that the defendant was making Lona fide claim to the property, and, therefore, .whether it was his or not, as be was actiog in the honest belief that it was his property, and mild net be convicted by them.—The jury found for the plaintiff, aud awarded him .£5 damages.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at Alforde Chambers on Tuesday. Present—Messrs. E. Carey (in the chair), T. Handley, D. Forster, B. Dutton, F. lieyes, J. Taylor, H. Gaskell ionr., S. Sadler. B. Brown. F. H. Pankhurst, Dr. O'Keeffe, D. Wright, W. T. Husband, J. Houghton, J. T. Allen (clerk), and Dickson (nuisance inspector). THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL. The Chairman said the deputation appointed by the Board bad attended upon the officials of the Local Govern- ment Board and discussed the plans of the proposed Infec- tious Diseases Hospital. The plans had had to be some- what modified in accordance with a recommendation of the Local Government Board, who had signified that they answered all the necessary requirements.

The Clerk read—a-letter from the Local Government Board stating that the provisional order with regard to the erection of the Town Hall and public offices received tilt Royal Assent on the 22nd July. The Clerk remarked that the London Board had previously stated that they would sanc- tion the bocrowing of the necessary money when the order received the Royal Assent, hut they had not yet done Co. Until they did the building could not be proceeded with.— On the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Forster, it was decided that the clerk, on receipt of the required sanc- tion, should at once instruct the contractor to go en with the work.

THE POLLIMON OF NETHERLEY WATER. A letter was read from Mr. Swift, clerk to the Huyton- with-Roby Local Board, raying the Board's communication with regard to the pollution of a stream at Netherley by sewage from the sewage farm should have attention. A CLAIM. Messrs Fawkes Brothers, contractors for the No. 2 main sewer contract, wrote under date the llth inst., inclosing a bill of extras amounting to £4B 13e 10d. They begged to inform the members of the Board of their intention to carry this matter into court if some favourable understanding was not arrived at.—The Chairman observed that the Board had dealt with this question on two previous occasions, and as them did not appear to be any new matter there was no rea- son why it should be re-opened.—On the motion f Mr. Brown, seconded by Mr. Taylor, the subject was eventually referred to the Sewerage Committee for further considera- tion.

div.head: SANGUINARY CONFLICT.
div.p: A SANGUINARY CONFLICT.

- - - - The Spaniard has or at least had at the time Lord Bacon wrote his essays, the reputation of not being so wise as he looked, while on the other hand the lively Frenchman was said to be far shrewder than a superficial observer might think. As a rule these very pointed and sweeping definitions of national character are not much to be relied upon, but now 11 and then incidents happen which seem to justify the popular belief that as far as the Irishman is concerned nothing is more congenial than a good faction fight. One of these incidents occurred on Sunday afternoon on Wilderspool Causeway, War- rington, when a terrific if not a heroic encounter took place between about a dozen Irishmen who were divided into two camps by the not very pro- vocative distinction that one half of them lived in the town and the other half in the country. The affray took place near St. James' Church, and ac- cording to the account of a chronicler, who de. scribed the event with an almost Homeric sim- plicity and vigour, the contest was quite sanguin- ary. The " onslaught "of the town warriors on the rustics was, it is said, "terrible," and "injuries were inflicted which will be felt for many days." One of the countrymen had his face so battered that he could scarcely be identified, and another who had passed into the "sere and yellow leaf" of life had his head banged mercilessly against a wooden post. At times the Irishmen fought man against man like Cireeks and Trojans, and at other times the battle was as indiscriminate as a "set to" amongst Kilkenny cats. One of the town Irishman, who may be described as the Achilles, or rather the Hector of the party, was anned with an umbrella, and the heads of his countrymen almost resounded with the blows he dealt them. At Jest, it is said, the fray was brought to an end b a powerful carter drawing away the town men, which seems to be a rather lame and impotent conclusion to so fierce a fight unless, indeed, the carter was exceptionally vigorous, or the combatants were satiated with the luxury they had enjoyed.

At this point the Fair Trader steps in and says--" yes, and to get out of this dilemma you must put 15 to 20 per cent.' ad valorem deity on all foreign manufac- tures." What we must put upon imported grain de- pends very much as to what sort of an audience the Fair Trader is addressine. If it should be an agri- cultural one, then 5s or lOs per quarter would be thrown out as a feeler; if to a town audience, then put a tax upon all manufactured goods, but on no account tax the poor man's bread or beer. What Free Traders are prepared to admit, is that agriculture is not as profitable as it should be, and that manufacturing is not pinch better off. The remedy is not to be sought, and will certainly net be found in Protection of a retaliatory or recriminatory character, but rather in making use of means that are already at hand. CRAM& AGAINST A RAILWAY POWlER.—Thomas Wil- kinson, porter at the London and North-Western Railway Station, was summoned for committing a breach of the peace on, Friday night, the 31st July.—lt was proved that the defendant was making use of most filthy language in Kent-street, to a worn an named Ann Cank, and the" neigh- boars were all up."—Mr. Knowles defended, and argued that the defendant was only making reasonable and due exercise of his voice, and using a littlo impure Saxon In conclusion he claimed the dismissal of the defendant. and Rose Kelly from the dock sent forth an earnest " Rear, hear," that caused Some laughter.—The B.ooii bound ovet the defendant to keep the peace for two months, himself in £lO, and two sureties of £5 each.--Ann Cank was then charged with a similar offence, hut she was dismissed, on the ground that Wilkinson had been the cause of her con- duct.

,--,, WARRINGToN _FARMERS' , 'Ctk, An adjourned meeting of the committee pf this club was held in the clubroom, White Bull' Inn, Hersemarket-street, On WednesdayarternoOn. Mr. W. Derbyshire (vice-chair- man) presided, and there WAS a good attendance of members. The SECRETARY (Mr. H. T. Stelfox) read the following let- ter which had been received in response to the memorial recently sent out to the neighbouring landlords, viz. : Wall Pit House, Stratton, Warrington, 10th August, 1885. —Sir,—Your circular of the 19th June came to hand on , the 29th ult. In reply to the same, I, as a small landowner, I have to say that 1 fully realise the fact that the present time is one of great trial to farmers, and that while in many instances their capital is being seriously encroached upon, the fact remains that should a farm become vacant ia this neighbourhood there is no trouble in getting a tenant. In conversation with a large farmer a abort time since, one of your members, I believe, he said to me : " I farmed in worse times than these and I can still make a profit." If it is not trio much for me to say, my opinion is that a per- sonal and friendly talk between landlord and tenant does more to establish a good understanding in reference to a re- duction of rent than a printed circular, and the fact that your club has found it necessary to issue such a circular seems to show that the relations between landlord and ten- ant are not quite on the footing they ought to be. With good wishes for the prosperity of your club and hopes that the present trying times—trying both for landlord and tenant—may soon pass away, I am, yours faithfully, CHAS, THOMAS WHITLEY.—I{. T. Stelfox, honorary secretary. Warrington Farmers' Club."—A :AMBER: I do not think ,t was a committee man who made the remark mentioned in that Ievee—ANOTHER MEMBER: I doubt the state- ment very much—Toe CHAIRMAN Said the statement was rather questionable unless there was some one more favoured than his fellow farmers. As far as he was concerned he never farmed in worse times than the present, though he had farmed in worse weather thin they had had this year. But he had never farmed when the price of agricultural pro- duce was as low as it is now, and the rents, labour, and taxes so high. (Hear, hear.) Therefore he thought the gentle- man referred to in the letter must be differently circum- stanced to what a good many members of the club are. There I were exceptional cases in which people seemed to think they were doing very well, earl he was only glad to hear it, but the majority of farmers, nearly all of them, were not in tbat position, and he thought it was only due that the landlords should know that farmers were losing and not making money.—Mr. WHITLOW thought if the farmer referred to was making money his farm would be growing worse. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. DAVIDSON said that if the farmer re- ferred to was a member of the club they would be glad if be would come and give them some advice so that they might farm with profit also. Ile was sure that they did not come there with a double face knowing that they were making money but they knew by the past, and by the stock-taking, which they generally made, that their farms were not doing well. If the farmer men- tioned in the letter was a in,mber of that cub, he was cer- tainly doing a very great injustice not only tc the club, but to all farmers and the -.:orninunity if he did not come and speak out like a man. He (Mr. Davidson) was sure that club would not have been formed had their farms been paying or had they been so that the), could live without their capital being reduced ; but they knew very well that they might go on for a few years by taking all they could out of the ground and putting nothing in, but the farm would suffer, and at last the farmer would come to grief. (Hear, hear )--lt was then proposed by Mr. KNOWLES, seconded by Mr. WHITLOW, and carried, that the secretary should write to Mr. Whitley asking him for the name of the member of the club who had said that farming was so prosperous.—Mr. Wurrnow : I am sure he is a proper man to read an essay on farming. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) —The committee then proceeded to discuss the terms of a second memorial on the rent question, which it was pro- posed should be drawn Op for the purpose of being for- warded to landlords. After a long conversational discus- sion the following was drawn up :—" That the members of the Warrington Farmers' Club desire to bring under your notice again the urgent need of an early re-adjustment of rents. Since forwarding you our last resolution we are now , in a position to approximate the value of this year's pro- -1 ' duce, and regret to say that in disastrous effects it will far exceed the eight preceding ruinous years. We desire re- T..tal :Phis match was-played at St.. farmers are fast losing their capital. PRE'SCOT.

PRECOCIOUS THIEVES.—On Saturday two little lads named Brownbill and Corner, between the ages of eight and nine years, were brought before Mr. W. L. Evans, charged with stealing a two shilling piece from a little girl who had been sent on an errand to the provision shop of Mr. Gore, Eccleston-street. Brownbill took it from her, and having got it changed, gave his companion sixpence, saving thit it was only a shilling. Having placed a shilling in his mouth he accidently swallowed it. They were remanded to the Sessions.

RE•OPENING OF CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOLS.—OR Sunday afternoon a flower and children's service was held in the Ebenezer Schools, formerly the Congregational Chapel, Eccleston-street, which have been thoroughly reno- vated and cleaned, and important structural alterations made. The flower service, the first of the kind, was pre• sided over by Mr. W. Evans, of Rainhill. Upwards of forty of a choir of children were ranged on the platform, which was tastefully decorat,d with flowers and plants, a white covered table being placel along the front to receive the flowers presented by the scholars. Addresses were delivered by the chairman and the Rev. James Johnston, pastor. At the conclusion of the service, the flO'Jent were sent to the Prescot Workhouse and Infirmary, along with a hand- some basket of grapes presented by Miss Evans, of Hurst House.

THE STRIKE OF Conanens.—The strike of colliers at the Can's Colliery, Whiston, still remains unsettled. A meet- ing of the colliers took place on jTuesday night in a field near the Potteries. The chair was taken by Josiah Hayes, cbeek-weighman, and a lengthy address was delivered by Mr. Woods, of Park-lane, agent of the Miners' Federation, who said that the union he represented had counted the cost and had determined to stand by the men of Carr's Colliery until the hand-riddle was abolished that was introduced last December. and which every reasonable effort had been made to have discontinued.—The following resolution, proposed by Mr. John Fagan, Prescot, was carried unanimously "That this meeting of miners in Whiston who are working agree to pey 31 per week towards defraying the expense of the district." It was also resolved :—" That this meeting is of epieion that a strong union is necessary in Prescot and Miami to protect our wages and position, and is hereby agreeable to bring about such an arrangement," On Wed- nesday evening the men on strike again received their pay from the Federation, at the Crown Hotel. A communica- tion heel been sent by the Miners' Federation to the pro- prietors of the Carr's Colliery, asking them to meet a depu- Winn, but no reply has been received. BE-OPENING OF EBENEZER CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL.—A flower service (the first held in the town) and a children's service of praise inaugurated the re-opening of the Cengregational Sunday School, Eccleston-street, on Sunday afternoon. The building, formerly used as the chapel, has been thoroughly renovated and cleaned and painted and important alterations made. The pews have been removed from the body of the building and replaced by reversible and open seating, six of the large old-fashioned square pews at the side have been retained for use as classes The gallery has also been partitioned off into four class- rooms, and a vestibule has been enclosed, framed in var- nished pine. The organ has also been cleaned and put in order. The large vestry is decorated and will be specially useful for Bible classes and small gatherings. The service commenced at half-past two o'clock, Mr. W. Evans, of Rain- hill, preeided. There were 350 children and adults present, and after the opening hymn, "In the vineyard of our Father," he gave an address on the " Responsibilities of parents and teachers." After another hymn he spoke on the " Privileges of children in the present day." The choir of forty childrn ore the platform, led by Mr. W. Pownall, organist Miss Brown; then sang "Buds and bells," during which the scholars presented their beautiful bouquets on a table placed along the front of the platform, their bright colours contrasting with the rows of evergreen and ether plants which formed the background. After the presenta- tion of flowers, the Rev. James Johnston made a statement as to the work and object of the Sunday school. After the service was over the flowers and fruit were dietributed amengst the Almshouses of Sewell-street and Warrington- road, the Workhouee, and Infirmary. Thanksgiving offer- ings at the door amounted to £1 10e. The school will be used for divine worship while the church is undergoing re- pair and painting. ODDFELLOWsHIP.—LOYAL FARMERS' NETT LODGE AN- NIVERSARY.—On Monday the above, one of the largest lodges in the Prescot district LO. Oddfeliows, M.U., ob- served their annual custom of walking in procession with the regalia of their order, and afterwards enjoying a dinner and dance. They met at eleven o'clock at the Brick Wall Inn, Tarbuck, between 40 and 50 formed in proceesion, led by the band of the Huyton Company L.E.V. Walking in front were P.P.G.M. J. Bixter (Prescot), P.P.G.M. Robert Wright, and P.S. Thomas Lawrenson, with their handsome banner. After visiting prominent members on the way, a call was made on Mr. J. Kenwright, Tarback Hall. They returned to the Brick Wall by half-past two o'clock, where the host, Mr. James Ambrose had ready an excellent dinner, to which 74 members and visitors sat down, including the G.M. of the district, W. Smeatham ; the Rev. Bro. Cham- bers, Rector of Haleviood ; Bro. Edw. Fleetwood presiding, W. and C. Gregory, J. Bustard; J. Wearing, T. Harrison, P. Lott, C. Wood, &e. The table in horse shoe form was laid out with taste in a marquee 80ft. in length. On removal of the cloth, and after the -esual loyal toasts bad been duly honoured, that of the bishop and clergy of all denomina- tions was replied to by Rector Chambers, who thanked the members of the lodge for their attendance at church on the previous Sunday. .V.P.G.M. Blot- ter gave an account of the flourishing state of the Order. Prov. G.M. Smeatham said that it now numbered 1,300, with capital £ll,OOO, or £9 per member.—Perm. Sec. Law- renson, speaking for the lodge, said that the number of members was 120, or an increase of three during the year ; four members had died, and three lapsed. Notwithstanding their having paid £lO2 144 63 sick pay, there was a gain of £23 133 2d, but he unfortunately had to inform them that since the balance sheet had been drawn the sick list had been very heavy, for £l3O had already been peid this year.—Toasts to the ladies, host and hostess, visitors, and press were duly honoured, and songs were interspersed, con- tributed by Messrs. Oscar, Rimmer, Wood, and Lawrenson. Afterwards the company was greatly increased, and dancing on the green, merry-go-rounds, shooting, and all "the fun of the fair" were enjoyedlto a late hour.

. - • WARRINCITON- ONSERVAT LYE CLUB. 6 OPENING OF THE BOWLING GREEN. s • On Saturday afternoon the bowling green at the Conservative Club was opened by Sir Gilbert Greenall,' iu the presence of a considerable number of ' specta- tors. After the green had been formally opened, a bowling main was playei, there being X 26 competi tors. The result was as followaz--lst prize silver cup, Mr. J. Shaw; 2nd, timepiece, Mr. HAbrook. At the conclusion of the bowling a number of the members at down to a dinner in the dining hall of the club. The chair was occupied by Sir G. Greenalls who was supported by Captain Reynolds, Messrs. J. Pierpoint, R. W. Franoomb, J. White, J. Roberts, J E. Wright, J. L. Whittle, W. Kerfoot,W. Hough- ton, and others.—. The Cilsraustr proposed the toast of the Queen and the Royal 'Family, sehloti haeing been duly honoured, Captain Raison:is proposed that of " The town and trade of Warrington." They must acknowledge, he said, that at the present time there was great depression in both trade and agri- culture. In fact, be did not remember the time when things were worse than they are now in this country, but he believed the period of depression was coming to an end, and that they would have much better times before long. Since they had last met together, a great fact had been accomplished, which must be of the greatest benefit to the town and trade of War- rington—he referred to the passing of the Ship Canal Bill. (Applause.) The carrying out of that work work would cause a vast amount of money to be spent, and would find emplOyment for a large number of men, and in the end would be beneficial not only to Lancashire but to the country at large. (Hear, hear.) —After a leer remarks from Mr. W. DIOICENS, the toast was cordially drunk.—Mr. CAWLEY moved a vote of confidence in Sir Gilbert Greene% which was seconded by Mr. R. Isnanwoan,, and supported by Mr. J. WooLF (of Manchester).—The CEttoncsN,, in responding, said he was pleased to see so many far- mers present. He lived among farmers and respected them, and &ally believed be spoke the truth when he said that the farmers of the neighbourhood reepeated him. He advised farmers to go to their landlords if they wished for redress, and not place too much trust in other people. Re also'arinonneed that he intended to take another ioo shares in the club, and • that his son, who, he hoped, would be long amongst them, would take 25.—Mr. JOHN ROBERTS moved & vote of thanks to the Conservative Association for having presented the prizes, which was seconded by Mr. Dzwnonsz, and carried.—Mr. Faattoomn, in pro- posing a vote of thanks to the Chairman, said that some of the people of Warrington might not believe in politics, but they looked upon Sir. Gilbert Green- all as an ornament of the town and an honour to the country. He believed that Sir Gilbert's title was given to him by the most far-seeing men that ever ruled this country.--Mr. SMETHURST seconded the proposition, which was carried, and briefly acknow- ledged by the Cumsdasiv.—Several songs were sang in the course of the evening, Mr. G. Riley acting as accompanist.

Secretaries of Cricket Ohms ere requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday mus-:, be sent tc .thehead office, Beersey-street, Warrington. not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

Caows C.C. v. PENKETH JUNIORS C.C.—A match was 'played between the above clabs on Saturday, Aug. Ist, on the ground of the former. Scare : Crown C.C., 66 ; Pen- ire:h, 45. PENKETII (4TH ELEVEN) V. TEMPERANCE STAR.—This match was played at Peuketh on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the visitors by 12 runs. Score : Penketh, Temperance Star, 34. NORTON PRIORY V. ST. PAUL'S. WARRINGTON.—This match was played on the Norton ground en Saturday' and resulted in an easy win for the Norton team. Score: Nor- ton Priory, 33; St. Paul's, 14. ARLEY PARK V. HIGH LE.GH.—This match was played Arley on Saturday, and resutted in an easy victory for thel home team. Smith and Rhodes bowled with great success,' Dale keeping wicket in good style. Scare :—Arley Park, 43; High Leigh, 18. PEOPLE'S COLLEGE V. ST. JAMES' JUNIORS.—This match was played on Saturday, on the ground of the former, and resulted in an easy victo,y for the College, owing chiefly to the excellent batting of Whittle (42) and to the good bowl- ing of Crompton and Dowd. Score :—College, 68; St. James', 12. • BRICK-STREET C. C. (WARRINGTON) V. CORNEROOK C. C. (MANCHESTER).—Played at Manchester on Saturday, the result being a substantial victory for the Warringtonians by 46 runs. For the winners W. Barton handled the willow very effectively, scoring 59 not out. Scores : Brick-street, . 93; Cornbrook, 47. ORFORD V. GRAPPENHALL JUNIORS. This match was 'played at Grappenhall on Saturday, and although Orford played with ten men, the result was an easy victory for the latter by 46 runs, with four wickets to fall. C. Grounds, W. Richardson, ind J. Thompson bowled well for the visitors, whilst the best batting was shown by J. Thompson, J. Smith (sub), and W. Richardson. For the home time, Idle's bowling was very effective, and S. 'Ellison batted the beet Score :—Grapoenhall. let innings, 28 ; 2nd innings, 47 ; total, 73. SECRETARY said that he had collected considerable informa- tion. As far as he was able to inform himself farm produce [ was paying fully 21 per cent, higher rates than those charged for goods of similar bulk and weight in other trades. '(A voice: Shame.") Farmers were really paving con- siderably more than any other people, and he could not understand why they did not move in the mat- ter, and get the railway companies to give them Justice. Farmers should speak out more unitedly on thrill matter.—On the motion of Mr. PERCIVAL, seconded by Mr. Weatioirrost, it was decided to recom- mend that the following resolution be sent to the members of the Cabinet :—" That the members of the Warrington , Farmers' Club desire to point out to Government that the preferential rates granted by the railway comptnies of the United Kingdom in favour of foreign produce are virtually protection for foreign as aaainst home produce, and they therefore earnestly pray Government to direct that the said preferential rates shall be inquired into by the Royal Com- mission on the depression of trade in this country."—lt was resolved, on the motion of Mr. A. BARBER, seconded by Mr. PRIESTNER, that steps be taken for a witness to attend the Inquiry and give evidence on behalf of the club if thought necessary.—On the motion of Mr. WARBairroN, seconded ;by Mr. BARBER, it was cleated to ascertain the cost of analysis of certain articles, and tke mover ef the resolution remarked that the club was not simply fighting about what some termed the sore question, but was working for im- provement of farmers in many ways.—This was all the business.

NOTES BY THE WAY. Cheshire, after defeating the M.C.C., met Lancashire on , Friday and Saturday, with the result that Cheshire were ' severely beaten. Here again Briggs was the most success- ful bowler, obtaining 15 out of 20 wickets. In the first innings, when the visitors were disposed of for 33 runs, his ' seven wickets cost only just over one run each, while in the second attempt be captured six of his opponents for 47 runs. In the second innings the Cheshire team were more success- ful with the bat, but before they can hope to have any chance against some of the strongest counties they will have to suffer a great many more defeats.—ln their match at Old Trafford on Friday and Saturday, Cheshire brought their season's engagemmts to a close. The successful objection of baths against Brown was a great blow to the county, as his services were much missed in the bowling department. The victories of the county have been over Leicestershire, Warwickshire, and Marylebone (twice), while they have been defeated by Lancashire (twice), Derbyshire, Leicester- , shire, and Uppingham Rovers. The draw has taken place ' against Derbyshire. The match between Derbyshire and Yorkshire terminated at Derby on Wednesday in a draw, greatly in favour of the home county. Derbyshire experienced their usual bad luck, having, when stumps were drawn at ' six o'clock, only 16 runs to get to win, with five wickets to fall. Surrey, on Wednesday, at Kennington Oval, gained a crushing victory over sornersetshire. With three wickets down no fewer than 368 runs were wanted to avert a single innings defeat. Messrs. Radcliffe and Hewett had made a good stand, raising the score from 76 to 184, and on Wed- nesday it was not until 205 that Mr. Itarlcliffa was bowled, so that altogether the two had put on 12q runs during their partnership. The last wicket fell for 251, leaving Surrey victorious by an innings and 301 rune. The Sussex batsmen at Brighton on Wednesday, with the exception of Mr Newham and Humphreys, made a poor show against the bowling of Wootton and Mr. A. J. Thorn- ton. In two hours and e quuter the last eight wickets fell for an addition of 124 rune, and Kent won in a singe in. ninga with 66 runs to spare.

A fall of coal took place and completely buried them. Sig MICHAEL Ulnas-Biwa AND WOMEN'S SIIPFRADE. —Sir Michael Hicks-Beach received a deputation at Bristol on Monday morning, from the Women's Suffrage Society and la reply to their memorial he said he was afraid he he could not say his opinions agreed with those of the depu- tation, for he bad always voted against woman suffrage. He, however, admitted the force of the argument that while they hal given to more ignorant classes the franchise, the injustice of depriving educated and intelligent women of the vote hal certainly been increased, and it was mainly on that account he took no part OR the last occasion when the sub- ject was discussed, in the debate or the division. Parliament had legislated of late so as to put husband and wife on an equality as to matters of property, and if the suffrage was conceded to those to whom he had referred, then woLld have a further demand on the part of married women. lie confessed he was not prepared to do anything which would give man and wife two votes. It introduced politics as it were between them, and would enfranchise all the women of Envland. THE INTEDRUPTILD CIDRISHIP,—A. large Dum- ber of persons attended the Petty Sessions at Newton Town Hall on Saturday, when the incident reported last week under the heading" An Interrupted Courtship" came on for hearing. The defendants, John Murray, a young man residing at Vitriol-square, and Alice Eyes, a young woman residing at Vulcan, were together summoned for doing dam- age to and spoiling certain oats, the property of Ann Wright, to the amondt of Is. There were present on the Bench Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, C.,Pilkington. and W. F. Gooch. Both the defendants pleaded guilty.- P.S. Cummins said: At five minute to tweve o'clock on Saturday night last I was passing an oat field at Winwick, in the occupation of Mrs. Ann Wright. I had my little dog with me, and it ran into the oat field and started barking very furiously. I immediately followed, and on getting about 15 yards into the field from the hedge I. found both defendants lying down in the oats. They had made a bed of eight feet by five feet, and had made a path from the hedge to where I found them, atad had done damage to at ;east Is. I brought them out and caused the matter to be reported to Mrs. Wright, and these proceedings have been ordered.— The Chairman : Who are the defendants ?—r.S. wins ; The young man lives in Vitriol-square, and this 1, young lady lives with her parents at Vulcan. She is sr:ry fond of being out at nights, is very seldom alone, and not always in the same company.—Ou being asked if they had anything Co say, the female defendant renßed that she had not, but the defendant Murray said : We only went out of the road of a lot of drunken men who were coming down the road. She was only about 200 yards from her own home.—The Bench fined each defendant 5a and costs, and ordered them to pay is each as damage. div.p: BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

_ The ordinary fertnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse Whisten. on Thursday week. There were present—Mr. Leatherbarrew (chairman), Rev. T. Finegan, Messrs. J. T. Hall, W. Birchen, J. Lowe J. Fisher, William Gerrard, J. Griffiths, Newsome, J. Mat- thews, T. Heald, J. Ellison, J. Agnew, J. Buckley, T. Dobell, T. F. Hill, E. Syder, William Swift, T. Eatock, P. Longton, W. Tyrer, W. Gore Ashton, and Hartley (clerk). GUARDIANS FOR ECCLESTON AND RAINHILL. The Clerk said, in accordance with the orders of the Local Government Board, two gentlemen had been elected to re. I present the townships of Eccleston and Heinlein. Mr. Jos. Ellieon had been duly eleCed Guardian for the Eccleston urban ward, and Mr. Thomas Heald, guardian for the town- ship of Italnhill.—A letter was read from the Local Govern- ment Board, intimating that they had paid to the treasurer ; of the Guardians £276 l9s lid, being a grant made by Par- liament in respect to the salaries of the Poor-law medical officers for the Union. INCREASE OF SALARIES.—A letter was read from the Workhouse master, asking for an increase of his and the matron's salaries.—lt was decided to send the application to the Finance Committee. THE MILK CONTRACT.—The Clerk said be had a letter I from Mr. Ward, asking for copies of the analyses of the milk sent for analysis.-Mr. Newsome said he noticed from the book that on the 7th July it tested 5 degrees of cream only: on the 4th august 51; which was lk degrees below the standard.—lt was resolved to refer the letter to the Visiting Committee. Tux COUNTY RATE—The Clerk said he had received from the county treasurer a precept requiring the Guardians to pay on the 29th of this month £8,579 13s 8d as their proportion of the county rate of this district. • THE INSPECTION OF GUT-DOOR CHILDREN.—Mr. New= some thought a committee ought to be formed to visit the children who were in places of confinement outside the home. He thought it was part of the duty of the Guar- dians to see that these children were properly treated.— A Member asked if they would be supposed to pay their own expenses 7—The Clerk said the auditor generally al- lowed 70 6d per day.—Mr. Newsome said that rather than put the ratepayers to any expense he would be willing to • pay his own —The Rev. Father Finegan thought the Guar- dians who came there really did a great deal for the Union, and to ask them to go anywhere on business of this kind and pay their own expenses was really asking too much, ' even for Guardians, who were supposed to be very chari- table. Hr thought the children ought to be visited, and he , I was of opinion the exp,mee of going there and back ought ' I toils paid by the Uoion.—Mr. Newsome said there was a Grin belief that some of the children who were placed out- side the district of the Union were not properly cared for, and he took that opportunity of saying that that remark did not apply to Pantasiph, but only to Kirkdale. It was a known fact th.et th, Kirkdale people were making 2s 2d out of each of these children.—The subject then dropped, and concluded the business of the Board.
LORD WOMELEY.—The Queen has graciously conferred the dignity of the rank of Viscount upon General Lord Wolselev, G.C.B.

THE ÜBALTH OF LORI CARNA.HVON.—The health of Lord CarnArvon is steadily improving. His Excellency left his bedroam for a short time On TuEsday. He will not, however, be able this week to undertake his tour to the West of Ireland.

THE GOVERNORSHIP OF CYPRXIS.—The Press Association understands that Sir Henry Ernest Bulwer, Governor and Commander-in-Chief of Natal, has been appointed governor and Commander-in-Chief of Cyprus, in place of Sir Robert Biddulph, whose tenure of the post is about to lapse.

'FATAL ACCIDENT,--NARROW ESCAPE OF LORD ZET- LAND —On Saturday evening an accident happened to a cab in which the Raid of Zetland was being driven from Bolon to Darlington, resulting in the death of the driver. His lordship's valet was also thrown off, but escaped unhurt. The horses bolted, and after going some dis- tance got into a h-dge. One fell and the other broke loose, which enabled his lordship to get out of tho vehicle unhurt.

div.head: SHALL WE REPUDIATE 'FREE TRADE? By H. WILITICI7I. _
div.p: SHALL WE REPUDIATE 'FREE TRADE? By H. WILITICI7I. _

It is quite possible, and even probable, that while we are considering the question of "Depressed Trade," that we are overlooking the, hot of our im- mensely increased output. Mr. Thonms Bart, M.P.. says :—" In the year 1873. a year of high wages for the miners of the Unittd. Kingdom, they produced 35.000,000 tons of coal less than they did in 1883, which was a perioZ of depression. Those employed were producing between eighty and ninety tons per man more than they were doing in 1873." In cotton hulls a system is being pursued, the end of which none can foresee. The °wont of 1883 was out of all comparison with that of 1873, and yet new mills are being erected, each one of which, it is said, drives out three or four old ones; that is, with each new mill comes new and improved machinery, manufac- turers stating that unless they can increase the out- put by at lease ten per cent, workmen will have to suffer. The more the cotton trade is looked into, and compares:l with the workings of other nationalities, the more it will be seen that it is not a question of protection, but a question of English manufacturers striving against each other in their race for wealth, anxious to make a fortune in a short time, and not caring for those they leave behind. If we look at the work turned out of forges and wire mills, the same, or a still more striking increase in the output meets us. A rod mill that ten or fifteen years ago would be content to turn out ten or twelve tons a turn, would now be considered an old fossil. From 20 to 30 tons a turn is now expected. This, coupled with the extremely anxious care that has been taken to reduce the cost of management, &0., has certainly given to the English rod maker a position as unique, as it must be satisfactory, in the way of making profits. What the increased output of wire mills is, betwixt now and twenty ago, would very much astoni.h all of us, could we only have it laid before U 9. We talk of "Depressed Trade," why, it would take three times the number of men engaged in the trade ten years ago to satisfy the present demands. If during the past five years each wiredrawer had worked after the old methods, and turned out the old quantities, the wire mills of War- rington would have been running night and day. One is almost disposed to say that Mr. Burt's advice to the colliers will have to be accepted by all, whether in mill or forge:—" If they worked rationally, and in a way that human beings ought to work, they would not at the present time have a single honest and industrious man out of employment." The Fair Traders, so far as I have seen, fail to take notice of this feature of the case.

It must not be supposed that all this increased out. put indicates increased profits to the manufacturers, Sir M. W. Ridley, M.P., one of the best-respected Tory members in the House of Commons, comparing. the trade of this country with that of "America, France, the continent, and other places that depen- ded upon the nostrum of Protection to save them, says they suffered from as great or greater depres- sion than we did," and speaking of the volume of British trade and its value says : If they took the value of the exports of the country in the year 1883, for which they had complete figures. and compared them with those of the year 1873, they would find that in the former year (1883) they were worth some- thing like 240 millions, whereas in the latter year they were worth something like 255 millions. If they looked further, at the quantity of the exports in 1883, and if they attempted to value them at the same •prices that prevailed in the year 1873, they would find that the exports in the year 1883 would, at the prices that prevailed in 1873, have been worth nearly 350 millions." Thus, we see that while British trade increases in volume, it decreases in value. That is not the only point workers must turn their attention to; while the urban population increases to an almost alarming ex- tent, the suburban deorefoes.

Whose only object was to invest their money, and leaving to others the duty of securing profits in a hundred eoneerne, while they themselves made life worth living.. How far all this may be true I caunot say, but. We have it before us and we must deal with it.

Gillespie, when Patrick Mannion, a horse dealer from Castlebar, County Mayo, Ireland, was brought me in custody on a charge of cruelly working a borne in an unfit state at Newton fair on the previous day. Inspector Lock- wood, of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty IS Animals, prosecuted. The horse was in a very poor condi- tion, excessively lame, and almost unable to move. The animal was exhibited to Mr. Gillespie, who said the case was a very bad one indeed, and the prisoner was fortunate in not being brought up at a Petty Sessions, when he would have been dealt with more severely than he would be; Under the circumstancea, as tbet was only an occatienat court, he would impose the heaviest penalty he could, and that was a fine of 20s and costs. In 1868 the Society of Arts issued a small collection of documents, theyesults of a scheme to which suffi- cient attention was nal; given at the time. A number of workmen had their expenses paid to the Feria Ex- hibition, and in return for, this benefit the condition was imposed that they should report in writing what they had seen and learnt. Nearly all branchee of in• dustry are covered in these reports, and nearly all agree as to the "admirable systems provided by other Governments for giving to their people systematic and univerally diffussi technical edu3atiot, and the deplorable neglect of such measures which has char- acterised the English people." Mr. Luoraft, chair- maker, speaking of ornamental drawing, modelling, and designing, says :—" Without the least doubt or hesitation, yet with the utmost profound regret, I say that oar defeat is as ignom nous, and I fear as disas- trous as it is possible to conceive." The lacemakers of Nottingham say :—" We are unanimous in opin- ion that French laces display a decided superiority in design and quality of material over the English goods." Mr. Aitken, of Birmingham, in his report, which heads the report of Birmingham artisans, says :—" Industry, formerly unaffected by foreign rivalry, contended only with small producers of its own nation, and then the competition was 5r1194. To be successful in this competition our nation must, therefore, put forward all its energies to educate, in technical and other schools, the present and coming generations." I couldn't hope to give a tithe of the reports given by these eighty-eight representatives of • the skilled workmen of Ea gland. Written's° far back as 1868, and confirmed in all particulars by the-Repert of the School Inquiry Commission, issued about the same thus, it must strike us all with amazement to think that one Commiseion'of Inquiry after another is appointed, and the results therefrom are so few. . _ _

one of the Royal Commissioners, Professor Tyn- dall, in his report, Bays:—" I have long entertained the oninion that, in virtue of the better education pro. Tided by Continental nations, England must one day, and that no distant one, find hers if outstripped by those nations, both in the arts of peace and war." Here we had, seventeen years since, the warning voice given to us to be up and doing, and yet what we have done has been so slight, that it was found neces- sary by the late f4overnment to appoint another Royal Commission, whose report has just been issued, and whose conclusions are almost the same.
With your permission, I will reserve for another paper further remarks upon this question.

M Arabs e the expression, "My shoe at you," as a token ,Of contempt. The same thing occurs frequently in this , country, only the shoe is used instead of the expression. le' ANOTHER EXPERIENCE.—SmaII boy: Pa, did you know i 'ma long before you married her ?—Pa: I didn't. I didn't know her till long after I had married her. "Oh, we will be so happy when we marry, won't we, Robert ?" "Yes, dearest." "And we'll have a nice cot- tage, and we'll take mamma along to live with us, and -" "Hold on, sis ! If you're going to take mamma along we must have two cottages." A lawyer walked down the street recently, with his length of arm taxed to hold a lot of law books. To him a friend, pointing at the books, said: "Why, I thought you carried all that stuff in your bead ?" " I do," quickly re- plied the lawyer, with a knowing wink," these are for the judges." "How did you come to get married !" asked a man of a very homely friend. " Well, you see," he replied, "after I had vainly tried to win several girls that I wanted, I finally turned my attention to one that wanted me, and then I didn't take long to arrange matters." A PLEASURE IN AarictrArrost—Mr. Dusenberry: Well, I've taken you to every place of note in the city.—Mrs. Dueenberry : Except to Laurel Hill Cemetery.—Mr. Dusen- berry: Oh, that's a pleasure I am holding in reserve! "Little boy, do you unde stand what is meant by energy and enterprise ?" "No, sir, I don't think I do." "Well, I will tell you. One of the richest men came here without a ! shirt to his back, and now he has got millions." "Millions! How many does he put 00 at a time ?" HE HAD SEEN THE PERFORMANCE.—" Are them real can- nibals?' inquired a countryman as he gazed on the wonders of a Milwaukee dime museum—'• real cannibals? Well, d'ye know what I'd do with 'em if this wa3 my show I" "No; what ?" "I'd starve 'em for three or four days an' then turn 'em loose on the rest of the actors. I just saw the stage performance." "Mollie, I wish you would be a better little girl," said a fond father to his little daughter; "you have no idea how son y lam that mamma has to cold you always !" "Don't worry about it, papa," was the reply of the little angel; "1 am not one of thou sensitive children. Half the time I don't hear what she says." As the late Professor Hamilton was one day walking near Aberdeen, he met a well-known individual of weak iatellect named Jemmy. "Pray," said the professor, "how long can a person live without brains ?" "1 dinna ken," replied Jemmy, scratching his head. "How auld are ye yourser ?" THE Foaca OF HABlT—Merchant: He was an excellent bookkeeper. He kept our books for many years in an ex- emplary way. I should have irq)t him at it —Friend : What did you do ?—Merchant: I made him cashier.— Friend: How did he do in his new position ?—Merchant: Excellently. He kept the cash. "The area of your country," said M. de Lesseps to the Russian Prince Orloff, "is almost exactly similar in extent to that of the moon." "The only difference," replied the prince, "is that, while the area of the moan is a fixed quantity, that of Russia is continually increasing." A couple of " innocents" waited upon the rector of the medical faculty of Heidelberg University. Professor : " What is it yon want ?" Both: "We wish to sell our bodies for dissection after death." Professor: " Very good; how much do you ask ?" Both: "Well, you see, at the University of Magdeburg they gave us each ten thalers 1" George had proposed and been accepted. "Well," she said. "I can sing and play on the piano and harp, can paint, and at school I was up in the floe arts and political economy and logic; and I crotchet beautifully, and play lawn-tennis, and, and—that's about all, I think. Now tell me what are some of your accomplishments, George. "I haven't any." "Not a single one ?" " Well," he said, with a sigh, "if the worst should come to the „worst, I might be able to cook."

ANSWERING A BLUE-RIBBONITE.—An anti-teetotaller who lives within ten miles of Forfar was driving home the other day with "just a see drap in his e'e," when he was accosted by a clergyman who advised him earnestly to bee. Sle a total abstainer, assurirg him that he would fled the change very beneficial. He was speaking from personal experience. He felt himself stronger, his general health was improved, and he enjoyed his dinner better than he did before donning the blue ribbon. The man beard him quietly, and then replied, "1 can see, sir, you had been a hanile far'er game thin mo. I can tak' my meat brawly yet. Gee up, Donal'!"

„ Auctioneer: ” But I say, there is nobody else in the room offering a bid for the ancient cabinet. How is it you keep on bidding against yourself r Broker: "Well, you see, that is a matter of business. I have got a commission from two different parties to buy the cabinet at any cost, and I don't know yet which of them is to have it." Rua TO LIFE.—" You're not looking well this morning,' said Mrs. Yeast to herhusband when he came down to break- fast. "No; nor am I feeling well either," was the ailing one's reply. "Headache IP' inquired the lady cautiously. "No ; but I dreamed last night that I was out at a large dinner party; and I must have eaten too much, for this morning I awoke with a violent attack of indigestion." " Trim's just like you :" exclaimed the unsympathetic woman.

A CAUTIOUS MAN.—lie was a mathematical fellow, and always engaged in making intricate cAculations on paper. The marriage was to take place on Friday; but he suggeet,d to his prospective mother-in-law that it had better take place on Thursday. "Why do you wish it changed ?" she asked, suspiciously. "Well," said he; "I have been making a calculation, and I find that my silver wedding will come on a Saturday evening; and that would never do, as that is the evening I have to go to the lodge." An attorney once came into court after having lunched too freely, when the judge said to him, "Sir, I am sorry to see you in a situatiosi which is a disgrace to yourself and family, to the court, and to the profession to which you belong !” This remark elicited the following colloquy : " Did your honour speak to me ?" "I did, sir; I said that in my opinion you disgrace yourself and family, the court. and the profession by your course of conduct." "May i-i-it please your honour, I have been an attorney 1-i-in this c court for h-f-teen years; and permit me to say, your honour, that this is the very first correct opinion I ever knew you to g-give !" LIVELY XIMES IN A COUNTRY Housn.—Mr. Frederick Gale, in his life of the Hon. Robert Grimston, says hunting was a passion with him, and his habit of fasting during the whole day when out with hounds must have injuriously affected his health. A witty old lady who was a constant visitor at Lady Verulam's house—where, during his mother's life, Mr. Grimston lived—used to say, "Oar dinner-hour is very uncertain, as just about that time, at least own a week in the winter, a servant comes and announces to .dear old Lady Verulam, 'Please, my lady, Mr. Robert has just been brought home on a shutter again!'"

FIERCE Arracx IN A WOREHOLISE.—Catherine Coleman was. at Liverpool, on Tuesday, committed for trial for as- saulting Caroline Wells, superintendent of the workhouse nurses. Coleman was an inmate, and was puniehed for misconduct. She met Miss Wells, knocked her down, and kicked her till unconscious. Miss Wells is unable to resume duty. The prisoner said in court she did not care what the magistrate did. She was sorry she had not given Wells more, but would do when she came out. DECREASE IN THE PRICE OF COTTON GOODS.—According to the Board of Trade returns, the total quantity of piece goods exported during the first seven months of the present year was rather greater than in the corresponding period of last year. The figures are 2,518,587,400 yards in 1884,and 2,540,227,200 yards in 1885, showing a small increase of 639,800 yards. But against this small increase in the volume of our export there was a drop in value from £30,114,696 to £28,482,460—a difference of £1,632,236. The falling off in value as compared with 1883 is more serious still. It exceeds £4,000,000, the figures being for 1883 £32,559,338, and for the present year, as already stated, £28,482,460. The loss is more conspicuous in the case of unbleached or bleached cotton. The export for the last seven months was 56,000,000 yards greater than in the corresponding period of 1883, but the estimated value was almost precisely £1,600,000 less. SIR C. DILBE, M.P., IN TILE DIVORCE COURT—It is -stated that a petition has been filed by Mr. Donald Craw- ford for divorce from his wife, Virginia Mary, Sir Charles Dilke, Bart., M.P., being the CO-respondent. Mr. hider- wick has, it is understood, been retained by the petitioner, and the ex-Attorney-General (Sir IL James) by the co-res- pondent. The following letter from Sir Charles Dilke has been recieved by Mr. G. W. 'Osborn, President of the Borough of Chelsea Liberal Association :—" 76, Sloane- street, S.W., August 7th.—My dear Osborn,—.l yesterday received formal notice of the commencement of legal pro- ceedings in reference to a matter seriously affecting my private character, the nature of which I have already com- municated to you. The charge brought against me is un- true, and I look forward with confidence in the result of the judicial inquiry, which must now take place. In the meantime I am precluded from making any detailed reply, but I am convinced that neither my friends nor my oppon- ents will do me the injustice of condemning me unheard. I have to request that you will take steps to convene a meet- ing of the Connell of the Liberal Association for this bor- ough, in order that these circumstances may be submitted ' for their consideration. If the Council should be of oginion that the interests of the party will suffer at the General Elec- tion by being confided to one who rests, however un- deservedly, under so grave an imputation, I shall be pre- pared to place myself in their hands, and to retire from all public life until this accusation shall have been disproved. It is with deep regret that I make this communication, and contemplate the eeverance, even for a time, of relations which have existed so long between the constituency of Chelsea and myself. I wish to add the expression of my gratitude for the kindnese and generous confidence I have received since 1867 from my supporters, and for the forbear- ance and courtesy extended to me by my political op- ponents.—Faithfully yours, CHARLES W.
