div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, TEITTRSDAY. At last! The turbulent life of the Parliament of 1880 is closed, and its records are added to new and momentous chapters in the history of England. As usual with Parliaments, of whatever character, it ' died calmly and without a struggle other than that necessary to bring about the prorogation at the earliest possible day. All the week the House has been in a lamentably empty condition. But that, i as everyone knows, s the best condition for carrY- ing on work, and it has been fully availed of this week. Meeting at four in the afternoon, the House I has on more than one occasion steadily remained at work for nearly twelve hours. By this means the most sanguine hopes of Ministers have been ful- filled, and at the close of the session they have an unprecedented amount of work to show as the re- Baits of the last four weeks. Of this last we shall hear a good deal at the general election, though probably Conservative speakers will omit to allude to the means by which success was achieved. But the public may be counted on to bear in mind that the legislation achieved was made possible by the removal of ail opposition in which Lord R. Churchill, Mr. Warton, and Mr. Healy were repre- sentatives, and the substitution of the Liberal party in opposition. Sir Charles Dilke has been in constant attendance through the week, and has taken a leading part in the debate on the Housing of the Working Classes Bill, a measure for which he, personally, is largely responsible. Much sympathy is felt with him in the circumstances that have suddenly arisen and threatened to blast his political prospects. When the story first got out, and instantly became the topic of conversation as mentioned , in this column , two weeks ago, Sir Charles momentarily sank under, I the terrible accusation. He withdrew from the House of Commons and went off for a few days to hide himself and his grief in the seclusion of Mr. Chamberlain's house near Birmingham. Remade no sign until the machinery of the law was actually set in motion. Then he took this, the first opportu- nity open to him, of publicly asserting his inno- cence, and almost pathetically appealing to the public to withhold their judgment till the evidence was before them. The whole of the circumstances of the story are curious. There has been no sudden and tragic dis- covery by an outraged husband. The lady in ques- tion is a connection by marriage of Sir Charles Dilkes, being the sister of Mrs. Ashton Dilke. Sir Charles has been on terms of closest intimacy with the family, and a short time ago exerted himself to obtain Mr. Crawford, the husband of the lady, who made the charge, an appointment as Boundary Com- missioner. It was Mrs. Crawford herself who made the communication to her husband, and he with singular precipitancy communicated with his soli- citor, and instructed him to take proceedings for divorce. It will be remembered that a short time ago Sir Charles Dilke addressed a meeting i of mem- bers of the Reform Club, and delivered an important political speech. On that very night, whilst Sir Charles was speaking, a friend who had heard from Mr. Crawford s solicitor what was about to take place was waiting in the hall to warn Sir Charles. He had gone down during the dinner hour with the cheerful purpose of straightway delivering his thunderbolt, which would have been a nice pre- paration for the speech Sir Charles had to deliver. Sending in for a membei of the club as a prelim- inary to getting at Sir Charles he was fortunately dissuaded from carrying out his original intention. Mrs. Crawford having made the statement to her husband has now withdrawn it, declaring it was made in a hysterical moment. Mr. Crawford, ap- parently, prefers to believe in her guilt. and accord- ing to present prospects the thing will be fought out to the bitter. end, Which is certainly the best thing that could happes in the interests of Sir C. Dilke. It is remarkable evidence of the advance, at least in the outward standard of public morals, that it should be generally agreed that, unless Sir Charles Nike is cleared of the charge hanging over him, his political career, now in the very rush of its tide, will be finally closed. It seems to have been different twenty years ago. At that time, Lord Palmerston being Prime Minister, a charge of adultery was brought against him by a man named O'Kane. This man had written to Lord Palmerston saying that fie had in his possession a number of letters that proved his guilt, and that unless money eompensation were forthcoming he should publish them. Lord Palmerston's answer was characteris- tically pithy. "Sir," he wrote, "Publish and, be d-. Yours faithfully, Palmerston.!' Rumours of the pending action were widely current just as they have been recently in the case of Sir Charles Dilke. But no one suggested that the Prime Minister would have to retire from a public career because of alleged laches in his private life. (Mane failing to get any money out of the plucky Premier, entered his case in the Divorce Court, citing Lord Palmerston as correspondent. The damages were laid at £.20,000. The case dragged on awhile, and Oliane finding it not likely to bring in any profit dropped it. Not the least curious feature in the - case was that at the time the alleged intimacy with Mrs. O'Kane took place Lord Palmerston was just verging on his eightieth year. It was only last week I incidentally mentioned Lord Houghton's name, and to-day he is dead. The marvel is that he should have lived so long, and above all that he should have been able to live in the manner that was most pleasant to him. He was in his seventy-sixth year, and up to the day he left England was never known to refuse an invitation to a dinner party, except where he had reason to believe the fare and the company would not be of the best. Nor did he confine his possibilities of en- joyment to private parties, where he would sit ' down one of eight or ten and take his dinner ▪ • quietly. Just before he started for Vichy, he dined . at the Star and Garter at Richmond, with the some- ' what tumultuous company assembled to do honour to Mr. Cyrus Field and submarine telegraphy. Of • late years he was so infirm that his man was in con- stant attendance upon him, walking behind hjm as • he went to his carriage, or lending him his arm when he ascended ,or descended a staircase. Like many old men accustomed to enjoy their lives, Lord Houghton resolutely resisted evidence of approach- ing old age. I faisey I have told in this column a story that illustrates this failing. But it will bear repetition. Going to lunch at his club one day in the Derby week, he found stuck up a list of the runners and the betting at a forthcoming race. He ap- proached it under the impression that it was the bill of fare, and his sight failed to correct him. "Same thing every day,' he grumbled, "roast beef and roast mutton, or roast mutton and roast beef; shall go and lunch somewhere else." • Lord Houghton prided himself greatly on his gifts • as an after dinner speaker. His last appearance in this capacity was at the dinner given to Mr. Ed- mund Yates. He then declaimed with many ges- tures what was doubtless a pointed speech, but the lamentable fact was that not even persons sitting • next to him heard a word he said. Still the per- formance had about it an air of true eloquence. I remember being present at a dinner where he pro- pe.sed the health of Mr. Lowell, then the American Minister at this' Court. Mr. Lowell, rising to re- s Pond, began his remarks with acknowledgement of the graceful and eloquent terms of Lord Hough- -1'3.11 S speech, Turning towards him to emphasise US remarks, he found out the noble lord, after his ulsitom in these last years, had fallen fast asleep. ay I, said Mr. Lowell, "interrupt my noble • friend's slumbers for. a moment to express to him my thanks for the manner in which he has pro- - posed' this toast." The old man sleeps now all tin- , disturbed, and with him has passed away a charao- ,• ter in which was mingled a haPpy combination of the man about town and the man of letters. If anyone wants to own a theatre now is his time. Tier Majesty's in the Haymarket, some time known as the Italian Opera House, is to be let, or, • !le- Crown lease may be bought. This theatre has nad a varied existence. The original building was Open 80 far back as 1705. It seems a long time ago, ut „is quite juvenile besides Drury Lane, where Nell 1,172t1e was performing in 1666. The Haymarket 17 Oil the other side 'of the road was opened in when opportunity was seized of enlarging Her Ma' 3S The house has been twice burnt down, • - ()nee m 1789, and again in in 1867, when the lessees were nearly ruined. The theatre was immediately rebuilt, but those connected with it were at the end of their tether, and the house got into Chancery. - Ten years ago the lease was sold to the late Earl Dudley for, I believe, £30,000. It has now about six years to run, and may be bought for a compara- tively moderate sum. The theatre has had its palmy days. But these are not of recent date. Rachel has trod its stair, and one May evening, nearly forty years ago, Jenny Lind, trembling and blush- ing, made her first appearance before an English audience. Jullien gave his concerts here, and Mr. Mapleson has, sometimes in open war, sometimes in days of truce, brought out Italian opera in rivalry • with Drury Lane. Homburg, I hear, is alreadsy very full. The season has begun rather late, and taus there was a week

div.head: EXAMINER SAT-VI-WAY, AUGUST 15, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SAT-VI-WAY, AUGUST 15, 1885.

or so between the departure of the Germans and the arrival of the English. Tar after year, this incom- patibility of simultaneous cortiminptionof the Hom- burg waters by Teutons and Anglo-Saxons has in- creased. It has now- come to this, that during the month of August there are more Germans in Folke- stone than in Homburg, and many more English in Homburg than in Folkestone. Even the doctors have had to yield to the times. Last year they allowed beer to their English patients ; this year they order it. So too,' they now admit, that the curative qualities of the waters need not be tested at absurdly early hours in 'the mbrning. Breakfast is permitted at a liberal half-past nine. The season promises to be good, but there will be many defal- cations. The irritability of the House seems to sug- gest that politics and gout go very much together. 'Homburg experiences point the same way. , gwitzerland will suffer more than Germany from the impending election. Its season runs later. On the whole, English watering places have again this year a great chance, and the cholera scare is all in their favour. Then there is another point which also makes for their advantage. I have not seen London so full of Americans since the year of the Franco-Prussian war. lam told that Killarney and Glengariffe are colonised by. them. We have them with us now—they and their dollars, and, unless the news from Marseilles should change, we are likely to keep them. The Americans have a dislike to cholera and a belief in sanitation. They are much too practical to admire the picturesque under con- ditions of dirt that facilitate the spread of disease. Paris will certainly be avoided, and for most Americans Paris is the key of the Continent. Regent-street and Bond-street may yet find that the disastrous season of 1885 had at the last moment some brightness in store. They have plenty of dry goods andsore in need of dollars. JUBILEE OF WESLEY AN :METHODISM AT WIDNES. • Come October and hhlf a century will have elapsed since afew earnest inhabitants of the then vil- lage of Widnes commenced to worship "according to the form of the people called Methodists," and the Wesleyans of the town celebrated the jubilee on Sunday by special services in Victoria-road Chapel. *Dr. G. Osborne, D.D., an ex-president. of the Confer- ence, preached two sermons, in the morning from Isaiah xl, 10 and 11 verses, and in the evening from Psalm xlv, 16 and 17 verses. In concluding his evening's discourse the rev, gentleman said :—"How little did he who took your first place of 'Worship dream that in half a century you wonld be worship- ping in a place like this; Sand as little did he an- ticipate the rapid growth and wonderful prosperity of your town. But it is well that you have been able to more than keep pabe with that rapid growth. I trust that the population willbontinhe to grow, and , that you will also continue to increase your efforts in respect to the furthering of your religion, and not I allow the population to get far advanced of you as in some places. I trust now you will show what I you think about the religion you have been taught 13y doing your best to extend and consolidate this work." Both services were well attended, the edi- fice in the evening being crowded. In the after- noon the Rev. R. Harper, the superintendent of the , circuit, conducted a "love-feast." Collections were made in aid of the Moss Bank Trust, and realised upwards of .£l5. Sunday's celebration, interesting though it must have been to all Wesleyans, is only intended, however, as a preliminary observance of the anniversary of the establishment of Wesleyan - Methodism in the town. It is suggested that in Qctober a demonstration on a magnificent scale shall be held, and no doubt every arrangement .will be made for honouring the occasion in a fitting - manlier. Fifty years ago Widnes was little more than an agricultural village, and to those Who are °nitrite- quamted with the Widnes of to-day it would be I almost impossible to picture the beautiful landscape presented to the view of our forefathers. Green meadows, orchards, picturesque plantations, and winding pathways existed where now are gray wastes, dingy brick buildings, and unattractive streets, while countless chimneys vomit forth day by day immense volumes of deleterious vapours, which have gained for the place the significant title of the black spot on the Mersey. There was, how- ever, already the dawn of future prosperity. The St. Helens Canal has been completed; a large dock has been constructed at Wood-end, as Widnes was commonly called, and the traffic waS considerable. Frequently the flatman and their families had to stay at Widnes on a Sunday, and Farnworth Parish Church was the only place in the vicinity where religious instruction and spiritual consolation were to be obtained. Mr. John Palin, the harbourmaster, an earnest Methodist who came from Northwich, determined that some provision should be made on their behalf. He offered his house on the Old Marsh as a meeting place, and arranged with Mr. William 'Holt, a "local "at Runcorn, who had won the ap- pllation of "Bishop of Runcorn," to conduct a ser- vice on a Sunday in the month of October, 1835. An I unforeseen circumstance prevented Mr. Holt fulfill- ing his engagement, and Mr. Abraham Leach, who at present resides in St. Helens, took his place, and can still recall the hearty manner in which the flat- men joined in the proceedings. A Society Class was formed shortly afterwards Mr. Samuel Halsall was leader, and Mr. John Palin and his wife Hannah were the other members. Months passed before the members were able to pay the first contribution of 2s 6d to the Warrington Circuit, upon the schedule of which Widnes first appears in September, 1836, as "Wood End." In Mr. Palm's house the preachers stood behind an arm chair whilst delivering their discourses, and this piece of furniture and a time-worn Bible are still retained in the family as valuable relics of the early struggles of Widnes Wesleyanism. After the lapse of two years the upper room of Messrs. Cooper and Hudson's sail-making establishment was rented at .E 5 per annum, in which to conduct the services, and Messrs. J. Potter, T. Stelfox, and Abraham Leach guaranteed to find the money. They were therefore appointed trustees. The sum of £3O was expended in furnishing the room, the money being raised in Runcorn by the local preachers. In 1837, the room was opened by Mr. Samuel Collier. In 1840, the population of the neighbourhood had con- siderably increased, and the Wesleyans established a school. The religious instruction was given by several teachers from Brunswick Sunday School at Runcorn, who granted a supply of old Bibles. lb will be interesting to learn that the ministers who preached in the sail-room were the Revs. James Laycock, Richard Rymer, B. Pearce, R. M. Willcox, R. Hare, and others, and the local preachers who have conducted services were Messrs. Evans, Geo. Hudson, Wm. Holt, James Cooper, James Potter, Abraham Leach, Thomas Hazlehurst, S. Collier, W. Hartland, and Dr. Smith. The society progressed very rapidly, and in 1848, Runcorn and Widnes dis- tricts were formed into a circuit, with Runcorn as the head, and a year later a chapel was erected at Farnworth. Mr. Thomas Hazlehurst, of Runcorn, contributed a large sum towards the cost, and about the same time he erected at his own expense a chapel at Ditton. The sail-room became inadequate for the worshippers there, and in 1857 a new chapel was built at Sutton's-lane. The foundation 'stone was laid by Mr. Thomas Hazleharst, who had given a very handsome donation. Prominent in the ' denomination at this time was Mr. Wm. Hartland, who had come to the town several years previously. He laboured earnestly and energetically for the cause, and he has been frequently termed the father of Widnes Wesleyanism. Sutton's-lane Chapel was used as a day and Sunday school until the formation of the School Board, when the depart- ment was transferred to that body. With an almost mushroom growth the town progressed, and the Wesleyan Society kept pace with the times. By 1864 Sutton's-lane Chapel had become too small, and Mr. Thomas Hazlehurst, with the munificient generosity which so distinguished him, offered, if the society would purchase a site, to build a chapel. The offer was accepted, and the handsome structure in Victoria-road is the result. In quick succession chapels were erected at Albert-road, at Hale Bank, and at Moss Bank, Mr. Hazlehurst bore the cost of the structure at Hale Bank. In 1869 Widnes had become so important a centre of Wesleyanism that it was formed into a separate circuit, and there was a cessation of chapel building for a considerable I period. In October 1879, however, the memorial stones of Lacey-street School were laid by Messrs. John Simpson, E. Carey, R. Shaw, and T. Robinson, and the building was opened in 1880, the total cost being £2,800, exclusive of site. A debt of £1,200 remained upon the school until January of the pre- sent year, when it was liquidated by a bazaar. A chapel to accommodate the population on the West Bank estate was erected in Oakland-street in 1873. It was also used as a Sunday school, but the provis- ion in a very'short time was insufficient, and the room had to be engaged at the West Bank Board Schools. It was imperative that a new structure should be erected, and in 1882 the society set. earnestly about the undertaking. Mr. F. H.-saos- sage, J.P., and Mr. T. S. Timmis, J.P., each promised £5OO towards the cost of the chapel, on the condi- tion that it should be named " trartland Memorial
I.th

. i Chapel," in honour of their valued s4ervant • and the staunch Wesleyan, Mr. William Rag-Lind. The offer was accepted, and the building which had cost £2,500 was opened early in ,1883 by the liev.,C. Garrett, then president of the Conference. This. is the last undertaking of the society, and it is a plea- sant duty to record that upon none of the buildings does the burden of a debt lie,or will not in the space of a few days. Such is a brief outline of the his- tory of the Widnes Wesleyans, who can celebrate the jubilee without one sad thought to cool the ardoit of their demonstrations. , , %ettero to et (fattor. , THE PEASANTS WHO WON'T BUY:' Sir,—lt is becoming clearer and clearer every day that the desperate attempts of dukes and earls and land-grabbers in genersl to raise up a puny array of pa Leant proprietors behind which they might continue unmolested to enjoy their inordinate privileges and unearned increments are des- tined to failure. We now learn from the newspipers that a considerable number of small plots of land were put up near Colchester for sale on easy terms to peasant proprietors, hut that no peasant came forward. This is as it should be. When the great landowners try to persuade the farmers and labourers to take a large portion of their land off their hands at a good price, it seems as though they had a very poor opinion of the "intellectuals" of those who have pro- duced them all their wealth. It appears as though they had said amongst themselves, "The reign of the democracy has begun, and the days of privilege and monopoly are numbered. Already the land monopoly is being questioned; let us sell out while we can or at least draw in such a num- ber to share in our monopoly that it will not be easily abolished, and above all, let us do this in the name of philanthropy and a Christian-like regard for our poorer brethren!' But it is evident the "peasants" have no mind to be made cats-paws of. They are clearly of opinion that land reform is in the air, and that the grievous social sores which are caused by the present system of land-heldieg are not to be healed or covered up by the poor plaster of a , peasant proprietary. JAQUES.

TORIES AND DECENT LANGUAGE. Sir,—The best thing in your last issue was Mr. Hamp- son's letter. In the first place he lost his temper, and this caused him to use strong language. And then he betrayed such an amount of charming simplicity that one wondered however he managed to screw his courage up to rush into print. All who know the gentleman are satisfied that sim- plicity and timidity are the two qualities for which he is remarkable. I cannot think Mr. Hampson is really the orig- inator of several of the words and phrases that appear in his letter. I fancy he must have submitted his first sketch to a Revising Committee, and they voting it too mild, in- itiated up3n their improvements (?) being inserted. First we have " Radical maliciousness." Why Radical ? Mr Roberts is agent for the Liberal party, and as such shotild he addressed. Allow me to say thetßedicals have too much respect for themselves to allow the intemperate talk of either Tories or Liberals to be fathered upon them. But what struck me most in Mr. Hampson's letter' was his remarkable foresight and knowledge. It is altogether a foregone conclusion with him as to what will be the result Of the next election. The working-men of Warrington are going "to return to Parliament their old aud tried friend, Sir Gilbert Green all, who is one of the greatest benefactors Warrington has ever had." "Prodigious !" Sir G. Greenall a "benefactor te Warrington !" Mr. Hampton is joking, or else doesn't know the man; but I suppose having an eye to the main chance he couldn't say any less, and I hope he won't use the word venomous " and " anonymous " be- cause I point this out to him. In what way does Sir Gil- bert prove he is a benefactor to Warrington ? Is it in the sums of money he gives to churches? A clergyman in this town told me not many days days ago that he would much rather not touch it, for he felt that a curse went with it. Can Mr. Hampson point out any special feature in which Sir Gilbert has helped the town since the advent of Baron Martin ? I remember immediately after that event, that superintendents of Dissenting schools, who bad been in the I habit of taking their scholars to Walton on Walking Days, were told to go to their Liberal friend, and I am confident that it is only since Sir Gilbert has been asked to become 1 the warming pan for his son that he has opened his pockets even to his own party. " Benefactor " Indeed! Could some fairy's wand chase the name and its "Benefactor," influence out of 1 the town, then indeed we should see how men Mr. lidMpSo/1 knew of the mind of Warrington working-men. I for one should very much like to know what Sir Gil- 'here's opinion is on the more important questiors of the day. lam aware it was quite sufficient for Warrington in the old days to know that in Mr. Greenall it had a member. lie not only could not speak in the House, he couldn't or wouldn't speak on cur local platforms. What does he think of Mr. Chamberlain's Merchant Shipping Bill? What does he think of the Free Education question? What does he think of the position Lord Iddesleigh is in with his premise to inquire into the present trade depression ? There are several things I should like to know Sir Gilbert's opinion about. For inetance what did he think of the meeting of the Tory party at which the political parson got up and made a Protection speech. winding up with a resolution, which " Mr. Coalman " would not second, but rather in all honesty told the meeting he could not be a party to gulling the people, by leading them so think that Conservatives were going to support Protection. Wasn't Sir Gilbert rather annoyed at the meet- ing breaking up in confusion? I rather think it was in con- sequence of his advice that the Captain waited upon Mr.lCoalnaan " and made alt.-Night by promising that the political parson should for the future eschew politics. Oh ! Sir Gilbert, I am afraid your party wants something more than a cry; it wants principle. Numbers of Tories confess that they see with sorrow their own party careless now as to what they shall conserve, eager only to get votes, whether It be by granting to Ireland Home Rule, or talking Fair Trade rubbish. PASTON.
"A BOYCOTTED LANDOWNER."

- - - - 81r,—Before the Assessment Committee on this Cale, Mr. W. Houghton made statements which are simply untrue, and behind my back when I was asked to retire for their consultation. This was hardly fair, if not irregular, as be is not on the committee. He is a man who lives with his mother sad biother, two bachelors approaching middle-t.ge. Such people are in some danger of becoming "puree proud." He tells the committee that this fault, in me, is the reason I have not let my property, and his modicum of rates is thereby increased. No wonder he Is alarmed. He is a neighbour I very seldom see, and he never speaks to me when we meet. He may be educated to speak for the family connections, which are very numereus, and occupy 10 to 15 houses aml farms very near together. I am outside this, the Bennett-Houghton circle. One of his nephews recently shot my retriever dog ; another always jibes at me. The Messrs. Bennett have benelitted much by having a great part of my produce at their own price—there being no competition where boycotting is the rule. They had my three years' hay crops at terms of One half for getting the whole ; no other offer could be got (though I employed an auctioneer, Mr. Joseph Taylor), except that Mr. J. Warbur- ton, Woolston, bid me £35 for the whole 54 acres. This, Mr. Bennett sold—his and my half together—in the stacks by the lump for £250, net cash, to Mr. Howarth. Mr. Ben- nett consumed his other two years' halves with his own stock. I have one of my half crops yet, boar years old, and have not been able to get an offer for it. I had to keep the only other half crop two years, and could not have soli lt then had not Mr. Bennett brought me a customer at £B5, or £4O less than my first half fetched, and which Mr. Ben- nett sold with his own it di, Quality and quantity the same, and market price. The above terms were so bad I resolved to hold out for better, and complained bitterly. The cones. quence was that I got no offer for two years, except £5O, nett, offered by Mr. Lowe, of Daresbury. Mr. Bennett seemed offended, and has had little to do with me since. This year, however, his son and nephew came and offered me £5O for the 54 acres of grass (or ditto to Mr. Lowe). I have all tithes, taxes, and rates to pay, which take the thick end off it. It was " Hobson's choice." these terms or rot again. It does not seem right that a person should have my produce at half its value, solely because I am boycotted. I could understand it going to some charity. I farmed the whole myself the three first years, and the three years' produce stopped with me so I was making a serious loss. and I was obliged to stop my farming. I could not have sold this three years' produce, had not Mr. Bennett helped me to sell it to Mr. Howarth, over our other joint sale to him, as stated above. It seems as though no one but Mr. Bennett dared have anything to do with me„ except by accident. The more buaim so I tried to do the greater ,was my sacrifice and grief. Still I persevered under this barbarocs infliction for years. Messrs. Buckton and Jeans let the farm to Mr. Ellisoa, and pre- pared an agreement to his approval, which he refused to complete at the last moment, without giving any reason. They also let it to Mr. Thomas Yates, of Padgate-lane, for his brotherein- law, and prepared agreement to his approval, which be refused to sign, or give a reason why. Business was nil, and a long bill came from Messrs. Buckton and Jeans, who wrote me saying, their "best efforts were totally , abortive," though they were under no restrictions. They advertised it to let by ticket or otherwise. Messrs. Bldg- I way and Worley have advertised and tried to let They , had applicants enough, and were not restricted in terms, but no business was done. One farmer remarked, "May be I shall he boycotted if I take this farm," and I did not see him again. It is not in my nature, I hope, to appeal against rates if not unreasonable, but as boycotting leaves me a large loss instead of a profit, I must try to put the blame where it is deserved. For the same reasons I am unable to let my Twiggery property. viz., a house of five b •droorrls, cottage, large warehouses, workehops, eteble, and 15 acres of land, chiefly osier beds. All the property used 70 let well till it and the owner became afflicted with the human parasites I hope to show them up if I live. I haYe never knowingly and intentionally injured anyone. Ii there are any who think I have, I shall be glad to hear from them. To make a fellow an outcast without telling aim what it is for is barbarous. I hope Mr. W.Houghton will nring a brilliant light to bear upon thismy "notorious case," is he advises the committee it is. Mr. Owen's report of 1883, to the 49 acres of land in Poulton, states the land "bore no .opearance of heving ever been laid down for permanent 9astnre." This description is quite erroneous and unjust. •.bout half of it is old, the rest mowing grassland; the rest armed on the rotation system, and is well laid down on the lttelevel, except one or two acres which are in hugley butte, nd not well cleaned. Mr. Bennett holds 23 acres precisely mailer land adjoining mine, and was re-assessed about the ,ante time at 26s per acre; yet Mr. Owen put 50s on mine— '

LAND GRABBING.AT WALTON." 81r,—It is quite evident from Mr. Hampson's letter in your issue of Saturday last that he has found it utterly im- possible to refute the statements made by me as to the con- nection between Sir G. Greenall and the closing of the Morley Common footpath. The present controversy arose entirely in consequence of the closing of this footpath, and when Sir Gil- beit's name was associated therewith by "Voice from the Crowd "—et which, bye-the-bye, I may say lam not the author—certain Tories burst into a howl of indignation thereat, and denounced the whole matter as untrue, malicious, &c., but upon further investigation evidence is produced which simply puts all these would-be defenders to silence, and in order to divert the attention of your readers from the main question Mr. Harnpson, "with that ingenuity and perversion of fact which is characteristic of the Tory party." sets up a very big man of straw, in order that he may knock bun down with a great deal of "sound and fury," and so call the attention of the public to his extraordinary accomplishment. Let it not be forgotten that- -1: Mr. Hampson has not disposed of the fact that an agent of Sir G. Greenall—Mr. T. Smith Burgess—wrote to the Railway Company requesting that the footpath might be closed. 2. Mr. Hampson cannot deny that Sir G. Greenall is the tenant of the land across which the footpath runs; hence the desire to close the footpath. 3. I repeat—in spite of the ravings of anonymous writers elaewhere-e-that Sir G. Greenall's gamekeeper is the only person who has interfered with the right ef the public to use the road in question. 4. If Sir Gilbert Greenall is the friend of the people of Warrington, and is anxious to show his utter disapproval of the conduct of his servants, why does he not at once re- quest the railway company to re-open this footpath? But sir, this is not the only case of the kind with which Sir Gilbert's name is and has been associated. Mr. Peers gives another instance—the footpath from Appleton to Hat ton. It is also within the recollection of many persons, that the then St. Helens Railway Company, now the Lon- don and North-Western, low level line from Warrington to Liverpool, appropriated a footpath which ran from the bottom of Bo'si-eareet into Arpley fields. Sir Gilbert Green- all was the chairman of the St. Helens Railway Company ao the time. A great agitation was created in the borough, and some time afterwards, during the mayoralty of Alder- man Burgess, the railway company were glad to make con- cessions in order to square the matter, which coecessions included the present cinder footpath all along the Walton branch line to the Arches, and the footbridge across the Arches en to the very piece of land where " our " footpath commences. Now, sir, this footpath question can- not remain where it is. I have little doubt that at the pro- per time the public of Warrington and elsewhere will assert their rights and the footpath will be re-opened. Although lam not anxious just now to occupy your space by replying to Mr. Harnpson's characteristic flights of imagination, yet from fear of being misunderstood, I must say a few words. 1. I quite agree with Mr. Hampson, that, as he was not here in 1880, he was not responsible for the Tory defeat which then occurred. I think Mr. Hampson's logic here is incontrovertible. Personally I am quite willing to ex- onerate Mr. Hampson from all liability for the Tory defeat in November next. 2. That as the "proof of the podding is in the eating," the Conservative gains of 1882.3-4 have yet to show them- selves. 3. Mr. Bowden's defeat was entirely attributable to the un- avoidable absence of our ward chairman and some eight or ten other prominent Liberals. The " Liberal forecast " is another delusion of Mr. Hampson. 4. At the last election of Guardians, out of 12 members returned for the borough of Warrington the Liberals re- turned six members for Warrington township and two for Latchford, whereas the Tories were only able to return four for Warrington. As regards the townships which Mr. Hemp- son says returned four Conservatives, no doubt he means Penketh and Newton, but as we in Warrington have no connection with these two places. lam at a lass to under- stand why they should be referred to, especially seeing that the elections there were in no way influenced by the light of Mr. Rampson's genius. 5. In regard to the South-East Ward, there has been no contest between the two political parties since 1880. In that year, owing to the help of the female voters, the Tory candidates were returned. Since then we have witnessed the edifying spectacle of the Tories fighting amongst them- selves. 6. As regards the election of assistant overseer, I can safely ear that neither Tory help nor Tory votes could have won or did win that election for Mr. Tunatall. I have the best authority for saying that if Mr. Tunstall had in the remotest degree depended upon the organisation of the Tory party he would certainly have been defeated. 7. In reference to the last South-West Ward election, cer- tain malpractices and the support of a concern haying no mean influence in the Ward, thrown into the scale in the interest of Mr. Jolley, proved too much for us. Now, sir, in conclusion let me say that I repudiate en- tirely Mr. Hampson's assertion that I have made "a mean, cowardly, and untrue attack upon Sir Gilbert Greenall." The meanness, cowardice, and untruthfulness are all on the other side, inasmuch as they (Mr. Haumson and Co.) are ut- terly unable to disprove one of my statements, and seek refuge in abusive language. As to what the working-men of Warrington intend to do at the next General Election—the matter will soon be set- tled. That there are solitary individuals whose politics change every time they get the "sack " and have to find a new shop, or for some other equally contemptible motive, I 11111 quite prepared to admit, bat they are few. Up to the present I have no reason whatever to believe otherwise than that the great majority of my fellow townsmen are as thoroughly Liberal te-day as they proved themselves to be In 1880. I believe that the Tory patty are deceiving them- selves, as the large number of their circulars which have been brought to ray office at various times by Liberals to whom they have been addressed woald seem to suggest. And now, a word to oar own fr:ends. It is quite evident that the Tories are bent upon leaving no stone (or mangle) unturned to win the next election ; it therefore becomes the more necessary that every member of ths Liberal party in Warrington should not miss a single opportunity of using any and every influence which he may possess to secure the triumphant return of William Crosfield. Warrington is a Liberal borough—it •nly requires the zeal which anieneed us in 1880 to ensure a greater and more enduring victory in 1885.—Yours, drc., H. ROBERTS.

THE PROROGATION OF PARLIAMENT. The Speaker entered the House of Commons at twelve minutes to two on Friday, when there was but a small attendance of members. A House was made at three minutes to two, the only Ministers present being Sir Michael Hicks-Beach and Lord Randolph Churchill. In reply to Colonel Gourley, Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL said that the duties et the Afghan Boundary Commission were not yet completed. It was not the intention of the Government to order its withdrawal, as Colonel Ridgway and other members were still doing useful work. The Go- vernment were not altogether without some confidence that before long they might be fortunate enough to arrive at a I satisfactory eettlement of the main points of frontier ques- tion not yet decided upon. (Cheers.) I At ten minutes past two Black Rod entered the House and desired the presence of members in the House of Lords ,to hear by Royal Commission the Queen's Speech read. I The Speaker. followed by all the members present, at once obeyed the summons. I At two o'clock, when the Lord Chancellor entered the House of Lords, and the Bishop of Truro had said prayers, there were only two other peers in the House, but dome of the lower benches were occupied by ladies and the end gal- leries were well filled. The Lord Chancellor, retiring for a few moments, returned with the Marquis of Waterford. the Earl of Coventry, the Earl of Lathom, and the Earl of Hardwicke, in their robes. They sat on the Bench in front of the Throne, and despatched Black Rod to summon the I Commons. The Sneaker, with many members of the Lower I House, having come to the bar, the Royal Commission was I read by the Clerk. and the Royal assent was announced to various bills. The Lord Chancellor then read THE QUEEN'S SPEECH. MI LORDS AND GIINTLNIIRN,— I am glad to he able to relieve you from the labors of a session which has been protracted and eventful. When you assembled in October last I informed you that an ex- pedition was advancing up the valley of the Nile for the relief of Khartoum. "Three months later, with a deep sorrow which was shared by all my people, I learnt that the expedition had arrived too late; and that the heroic General Gordon and his companions Lad fallen. An endeavour, which was ineffectual, was made to reach Khartoum by constructing a railway from Suakim to Berber. My troops were ultimately withdrawn from the whole of the Eastern Soudan, except Souakim, and from the Western Soudan down to Alashkert. Although the objects of the expedition have not been attained. I have great reason to be proud of the bravery and endurance which have been display ed by my soldiers and sailors, I and of the skill with which they have been commanded I received with great pleasure loyal offers of military as- sistance in this campaign from my colonies and from the native princes in India ; and a contingent from the colony of New South Wales served with distinction in the actions which took place on the coast of the Red Sea. The death of ' the alandi will probably enable me to perform with less difficulty the duties towards the ruler and people of Egypt, which events haye imposed upon me. I shall not relax in my efforts to place the Government and good order of the country upon a firm foundation. My relations with other powers are of a friendly nature. Difficul ties, which at one time were of an anxious charac- ter, arose between my Government and that of Russia as to the limits of the territory of my ally, the Ameer of Afghan- istan. Negotiations still centinue, and will, I Crust, lead at an early period to a satisfactory settlement. The progress of events in South Africa has compelled me, in the interests of the native races, to take under my pro- tection Bechuanaland and certain adjacent territories. I am taking the necessary steps to place the north-west frontier of my Indian Empire in a condition of adequate defence, in the absence of which the prosperity and tran- quility of my Indian subjects are liable from time to time to be interrupted and disturbed.

GRIMM:RR OF TIM HOUSB OF COMMONS— I thank you for the liberality with which, during the past year, you have provided for the services of the coun- try. DIF LORDS AND GENTLRMEN I have had pleasure in giving my assent to a measure for enabling federal action in certain matters to be taken by the Colonies of Australasia, to a much needed amend- ment of the criminal law, and to a bill for establishing a new department of Scottish affairs. I have also been glad to concur in a measure for increas- ing the number of occupying freeholders in Ireland. I notice with sincere gratification that an endeavour has been made by a Bill, to which I have assented, to disainish the evils of overcrowding and of insanitary dwellings, which hinder so seriously the moral and material well-being of the labouring classes. I regret to say that the depression which has so long prevailed in many important trades, and in the agricul- tural and manufacturing industries of the country, still continues. I have directed the issue of a Commission to in- quire into the causes of it, aud to ascertain whether it can be alleviated by any legislative measures. During the past session your time has been principally occupied by the enl trgement of the electorate, and the ex- tensive changes which you have in consequence made in the constitution of the House of Commons. I earnestly trust that these comprehensive measures may increase the efficiency of Parliament, and may add to the contentment of my people. It is my purpose before long to seek their counsel by a dissolution of Parliament. I pray that the blessing of God may rest upon their ex- tended liberties, and that the numbers who are called to the exercise of new powers will use them with the sobriety and discernment which, for so long a period, have marked the history of this nation. The Lord Chancellor next directed the reading of the commission proroguing Parliament formally until the 31st of October. The Speaker and members of the House of Commons then retired, and the House rose for the recess. The Speaker returned to the House of Commons at twenty-five minutes to three, and proceeded to read the Royal Speech, all the members present sitting uncovered. On the conclusion of the reading of the Queen's Speech, the members of the Government including Sir Michael Hicks-Beach end Lord Randolph Churchill, filed past the Speaker's ch dr and shook hands with the right hon. gentle- man. Several of the members of the Home Rule party walked out of the House without joining in the concluding act of the ceremony. Thus ended at twenty minutes to three the eixth session of the ninth Parliament of her Majesty Queen Victoria.

John Soholes, foreman joiner, of Hill House, died at Huddersfield Infirmary on Thursday morning. This is the fourth death from the recent accident at the railway station.

The Queen has been pleased to appoint the Duke of Richmond and Gordon, President of the Board of Trade, to be Secretary of State for Scotland, with a seat in the Cabinet. , By 22 votes to 15 the Liverpool City Council has resol- ved to open during cert tin hours on Sunday, for one year, the local museum and gallery of art and the public I free library. I Mn. J. E. BARLOW, the Liberal candidate for the Knutsford Division, will give an address at the 1 Temperance Hall, Latchford, on Tuesday next. Mr, W. Long, J.P., is announced to preside, and amongst i, other gentlemen expected to take part in the pro- ceedings are Mr. C. Broadbent, J.P., Mr. Ziba Armi- tage; J.P., and Mr. Frank Roberts. We trust that the Liberals of this district will rally round the candidate who is fighting their battle, and record him a hearty reception.

THE ‘VIDNES HORSE STEALING CASE.—THE PRISONER COMMITTED. Henry Beard, farmer, Upton Rocks, near Widnes, was brought before Mr. J. Brock, at Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, charged on remand with having, between 10 o'clock on Monday night the 3rd inst„ and eight o'clock the following morning, stolen a roan horse worth £7O, belong- ing to Mr. Peter Hodgkinson, farmer, Stockshouse Far,n, Cronton.—Mr. McKenzie, solicitor, Prescot, represented the prisoner—The prosecutor said the roan horse now in the police yard was his property. It was safe between eight and nine o'clock on the 3rd inst., and he missed it next morning. The prisoner knew the horse well.—Frank her- foot, farmer, Sankey, said about four o'clock on the morning of the 4th August he was going along Liverpool- road to St. Helens market. When near Sankey Chapel he I met the prisoner riding on a brown mare and leading a roan I hone. He had known the prisoner for a year or two.— John Hodge, railway porter, Central station, Warrington, who lives at 23. Heaton-street, Warrington, deposed to the prisoner bringing the horses to the Warrington Central station about seven o'clock on Tnesday morning, and book- ing them for Doncaster. They were despatched by the 9-6 a.m. train and the prisoner accompanied them.—llenry liodgkinson, son of the prosecutor, stated that the-prisoner had seen him with the roan horse many score of times.— William Wood, railway porter, Doncaster, gave evidence as to the arrival of the animals at Doncaster in the afternoon, and handing them over to the prisoner, who produced an invoice and claimed them. The prisoner got a Doncaster man named Shepherd to assist him to take them away.— P.S. Bonny, Doncaster, stated that in consequence of a tele I gram received, he went to the White Bear Inn yard, Don- caster, on the afternoon of the 4th. There is a blacksmith there. He saw the brown mare and a roan horse, the for- mer being held by Shepherd, and the latter by the prisoner. He inquired who the horses belonged to, and the prisoner replied "mine." lie took the prisoner into custody on a charge at stealing the horses, and he replied "I am very sorry if you do, I bought them at Warriegton." He gave the name of "Beer," and said he came from Fern- worth. At the time he went into the blacksmith's shop, one of the horses had been shod and the other was ibeing re-shod. With the permission of the prisoner ha paid the blacksmith ss, and the man Shepherd 2e 6ti. Next morning he gave prisoner and the horses into the custody , of P.C. Thompson.—P.C. Thompson deposed that from in- formation received he went to Warrington an Tuesday morn- ing the 4th inst. In consequence of inquiries of the rail- way officials at the Central Station he wired ter the railway officials and the police authorities at Doncaster with refer- ence to the horses. He went to Doncaster by the 2-25 train, and at the police station there found the horses for which he was in search. The prisoner was in custody. He brought the prisoner and the horses to Widnes next day. The prisoner said "I booked the horses at Warrington to Doncaeter, and received them there. The bridle on the mare is mine. I put it on because she broke the halter at Warrington." When charged with stealing the roan' horse, prisoner replied "Not so."--Edward joiner. Upton Rocks, deposed to meeting the prisoner at half-past eight on the previous evening of the 3rd inst. at a 1 wicket gate leading to the prosecutor's field. He did not notice any horse in the field. He had known the prisoner four or five years. The foothpsth was the prisoner's direct way home.—The prisoner was then charged in the usual fashion, and through his solicitor said he reserved his de- fence.—The prisoner was then charged with having between the same times, stolen a dark bay mare, worth £6O, the property of Mr. Thomas Corns, farmer, Hough Green, Dit- ton.—The prosecutor stated the mare was safe in a field near Stone-lane at ten o'clock on the night of the 3rd inst. The animal had gone at half-past five next morning. The pri- soner nor no one else had a right to take it. The prisoner knew the mare.—The evidence given in the previous case was then repeated, and the prisoner was committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions, bail being refused.

div.head: LOYAL ORDER OF ANCIENT SHEPHERDS.
div.p: LOYAL ORDER OF ANCIENT SHEPHERDS.

On Saturday the members of the " Pride of Latchford Lodge, in connection with the Warrington District (Ashton Unity) celebrated their annual gathering by partaking of a dinner at their lodge-house (Bro. Ireland's), the Cheshire Cheese Inn, Latchford. After dinner, the Pro. C.S. of the district (Bro. John Scattergood) was voted to the chair ; W.M. Thomas Chorlev occupying the vice-chair. There were also present D.P.C.S. Arthur F. J. Potter, Pro. Cor. Sec. Abel H. Mather, Lodge Surgeon Dr. James Cannon, P.M. John Murphy, Treasurer Peter Kirkham ; Messrs. Jchn Burgess (National Order of Oldfellows), J. Hartley, Thomas Barber, and others. After the usual loyal toasts had been honoured, the Chairman remarked that he was glad to be able to say that, notwithstanding the past year had been a very expensive one in the way of payments for sickness and death, the Order was in a prosperous crreli- tion.—" The Warrington District " was proposed by P.M. 'lsaac Jones; and in response the Pro. Cor. Sec. stated that the payments for the year 1894 had been very heavy, the 1, sum of £685 23 10d having been paid for sicknesa, and for deaths £l9O. The increase in payments over the year 1883 was £llO 163 4d. Notwithstanding the fact that the expenditure had been so great, the income had enabled them to meet all claims, and to add to their funds the SUM of £73 6s 41d, making the total worth of the district £2,695 17s op. (Applause.) The number of members at the commencement of the year was 955 ; admitted during the year, 102; suspended and lost by death,. OS; making the total number of members 959, or an increase of 4. (Applause.)—" The Pride of Latchford Lodge" was re- sponded to by Secretary, Isaac Jones, who congratula- ted the members on their prosperous condition, and stated that they had paid for sickness during the past year the sum of £2O Os sii, leaving the lodge now worth a little over £5O, which he thought was very gratifying when they considered the short time the lodge had been established. (Applause.)—P.M. James Burgess, in suitable terms, pm- posod the health of the lodge surgeon; and Dr. Cannell re- sponded.—" The hoe Members " was responded to by Bro. T. Barber.—A vote of thanks to the host and hostess WWI moved by Brother P. Kirkham, and Brother Ireland suitably responded.—ln the course of the evening songs were sung by Messrs. John Burgess and P. M. Millington ; and Bros. Barber and Ball, and others.

LATEST- It is expected that the Egyptian cotton crop will he very abundant. The worst symptoms in Mr. Ruskin's condition contirme. Ha suffers from sleeplessness. The three battalions of Guards now at Cyprus will shortly be ordered to England. Lord Ernest Vane Tempest, third son of the Marquis ef Londonderry, died at Scarborough on Friday. Baron Ferdinand de Rothschild has remitted fifteen per cent. of the tenants rents on the Buckinghamshire estates for the next three years. At Dudley Board of Guardians meeting on Friday it was stated that great distress prevailed in the district owing to the stoppage of ironworks and collieries. Work has been resumed in three large cable factories in South Staffordshire, the employers having conceded an ad- vance. The men have been idle for three months. The Central News says the statements that the Duke of Edinburgh has been appointed to succeed Lord John Hay in command of the Mediterranean squadron are erroneous. At Bilston, on Friday, Sarah Betsy Hill, a single young woman, aged 18, was charged with the wilful murder of her newly-born illegitimate child. She was committed for trial. On Friday there was some abatement of the storm which has raged for three days on the Scotch north-east coast, but 200 Fraserburg boats are still missing, and the anxiety of the fishing population is unbounded. MURDER OF A KEEPER —A brutal murder is supposed to have been committed in Blenheim Park, Woodstock. A keeper named Wm. Bickley, aged 64, was found on Friday 1 with his head cat in a dreadful manner. A man named George Boddington, with whom the deceased had worked, has been arrested, it being stated that he had quarrelled, with the deceased. THE OLDHAM STRIKE—The fourth payment of strike money was made on Friday. The number of recipients is about 3,400 spinners and twiners, or over half the niembere of the union. Members are receiving a shilling for over 4,000 children. There are nearly 3,000 full time piecers and 500 half timers receiving pay. The number of persons who are receiving any remuneration is over 15,000. Mr. Hib- bert, M.P. for Oldham, has written a letter in which he sug- gests a settlement by arbitration. FATAL OUTRAGE BY A DEAF MUM—At Uxbridge, on Friday. George Baker, tailor, of Harleston, Norfolk, who Is de if and dumb, was charged" with causing the death of a woman, named Mary Plurnmeridge, aged 76, on Thurs- day evening. The accused, who only arrived in Uxbridge on Thursday evening from Watford, quarrelled with a woman in the Checker's-yard, and the deceased interfered. It is alleged that Baker attacked her, and throttled her so severely that she died. He was remanded until Monday after formal evidence. EIGHT FRENCH EXCURSIONISTS DROWNED. Pants, FRIDAY.—A telegram received here states that a boat capsized off Royan this afternoon. Eight excur- sionists, including four women, were drowned. SIR H. D. WOLFF'S MISSION. Cauca, FRIDAY.—Sir H. Drummond Wolff is not ex- pected to arrive here before September 15. After his arrival he will, in all probability, proceed to Wady Haifa. THE AFGHAN QUESTION. PARIS, FRIDAY.—A telegram received here from St. Petersburg of to-day's date states that the Russian Govern- ment, in regard to the Zulficar question, has despatched pro- posals to London, to which the assent of the British Govern- ment appears certain. THE SEIZURE OF THE CAROLINE ISLANDS BY GERMANY. A Central News telegram, dated Madrid, Friday morning, says :—The intelligence of the seizure of the Caroline Islands by Germany creates much excitement here' not- withstanding the all-absorbing attention claimed by the cholera. The Cabinet have dispatched apr )test to Merlin, and have directed that two war vessels at present at Manila shall preceed to the igen& at once.
